utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on which date were you evacuated from the area of Eastern Slavonia and when did you go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not evacuated from Eastern Slavonia. After the 16th of September, when I was taken prisoner, I was transported to Serbia, and from there we joined a convoy in Sremska Mitrovica and I think we left Sremska Mitrovica on the 19th or 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The interpreters did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the date when you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left Vukovar, I think it was the beginning of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you were in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then we were taken through Serbia to Mitrovica. So I was in Mitrovica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've lost all sense of time by now, so I can't say how many days it was, but in the prison itself, the prison in Mitrovica, I think it was about six days, five or six days, up to seven. I can't say exactly. I can't say the exact number of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when you were transported to Serbia, you were transferred from an area where there were conflicts to an area that was peaceful and where you were safe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not safe. As a matter of fact, we were -- we had an armed escort, the army, the police, and you cannot really talk about safety in that sense. What does that mean? What kind of safety is that when you are there under force, when you are being driven by them and you don't know where they are driving you and how long this will last. So one cannot speak about safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 5, in paragraph 3, you say that an officer of the JNA, Brigadier Zoric, addressed your group. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we came to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that my microphone was not on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what this man was by rank? Because in the JNA there is no such rank as "brigadier."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not familiar with ranks. I said "brigadier," but at any rate, he wore a military uniform. He was not a plain soldier, he was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When he spoke to you, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we had already met him in Sremska Mitrovica -- or rather, in Sid, in Mitrovica he said that we would stay there. There were young children with us. The youngest child was about one year old. I think that some of the women asked what they would do with their children when we realised that we were within prison walls, and he said what did we want? Think of what the Ustasha were doing with the Serb women and children, and then he talked about Yugoslavia and the army, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he offend you in any way, insult you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What offended us was that he addressed us in such a way, that all of us who were brought there were Ustashas from that youngest child up to the oldest woman who was there. However, nobody said anything. We were all silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that he thought that you were all Ustashas, starting from that youngest child up to the oldest woman? Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how they spoke about Croats who were there in their captivity, in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In this same paragraph that I quoted, you say that in the JNA bus that transported you there were two Chetniks sitting on the two seats behind the driver. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me find this section.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've already quoted that paragraph to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were always men who were armed, who sat at the front seats. They wore uniforms, and they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did they wear, these two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Olive green-grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So why did you use the word "Chetnik" if they were JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not young soldiers. These were older men, and they kept playing songs to us over the loudspeakers. That's why I said they were Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were songs that they played to you on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, their entire behaviour towards us was that way. At any rate, I didn't think that they were soldiers who were behaving according to military rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they offend you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never spoke to us. They never communicated with us in a normal way. It was always in an insulting way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any of that? Can you describe any of these things that were insulting when you say they drove you on that bus and they were sitting behind the driver? What were the ways in which they offended you, insulted you, since they did not address you, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that journey, it was very, very hard. We felt unsafe. It was tough for us. We stopped in a town and a group of people walked up to the bus and they started rocking the bus. Everything that was happening to us and around us was more than terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the soldiers did not allow anyone to harm you in any way or to do anything to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they allowed it or not. We spent some time there, when this group of people happened to be around the bus. Now, I don't know whether they knew who we were, but they were intimidating us and then the bus went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that when you arrived in Becej you were examined by a doctor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that you were put up at the kindergarten; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6, paragraph 3, you say that in the kindergarten you were visited by a certain Sveto. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you understood that he was a member of the state security, judging by your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the very beginning. But as we were there and as he told us that he was in charge of us and we were locked up there, we were not allowed to go out at all, he would come to see us, and I don't know how it was that somebody found out that there were some people from Vukovar and some civilians showed up and then he put us into a room. He put a pistol on the table. He asked to say who it was that said that we were from Vukovar. After that, the International Red Cross was there and then he was with the members of the then-state security. They questioned us and he put us on the buses, and he said before the Red Cross appeared, he said that if anybody said anything else, we would all end up in the woods, all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of us who were there. He was not in uniform. That's why I said that he was from state security. He didn't say anything. But judging by how things were developing, I came to the conclusion that he came from state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this man was upset that somebody had said that you were from Vukovar, because he was afraid that because of the things that were going on in Vukovar this might cause some trouble, that could put you in harm's way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that he was afraid that there would be any trouble, because otherwise he would not have said that if anybody said anything else, we would all end up in the woods and nobody would know what happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify that, but from what I can see in your statement, page 6, paragraph 4, while you were staying in Becej, you were visited by representatives of the International Red Cross. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were asked to write down the names and telephone numbers of persons in Serbia or in Bosnia that you wanted to go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that they asked us for that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think I saw that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. That relates to Sremska Mitrovica, Your Honours, and not to Becej.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, in Sremska Mitrovica. Did they ask you to give the names and telephone numbers of persons you wanted to go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened only at the sports hall in Sremska Mitrovica. After we were transported there by buses from the prison. It was at the sports hall where we met the people who had come from Vukovar. But I remember that only Bosnia was mentioned. I don't know whether anybody had anyone in Serbia, but that is what we were asked to do, to give a name and address, telephone number. But this was only at the sports hall in Sremska Mitrovica, not in prison. In the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spent a few days in total in Serbia from the moment you arrived and when you were -- until you were sent away in this convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen from my statement. I don't know whether it was a total of 10 days or 12 days. It can be seen from the statement. I really made an effort to try to remember every day when they were transporting us from one place to another, but I had lost all sense of time, what day it was and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I assume that you understand whether this convoy was being prepared, whether there was some kind of a preparation procedure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were transferred to Bosnia and then to Croatia in Djakovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So then they gathered you all there at the sports hall and from there they organised convoys and through Bosnia you arrived in Djakovo in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that we did not come in a convoy. We are a group of women and children that was taken from Vukovar to Serbia and we came from the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. We were not in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But from this sports hall, since you were brought there to this sports hall, then you were transported through Bosnia to Croatia and Djakovo in a convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with all the people who had come there, this large group of people that had come there to the sports hall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now the microphone is on. Tell me now, what about you and the members of your group? Were you beaten or mistreated in any way while you were in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no physical mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear of anyone perhaps being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, while we were all there, while we were in prison, there was absolutely no information coming our way as to what was going on. Everything I heard I heard after I had come to Croatia and after we became free again. I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA organised a convoy there, that's what you're saying, and then you who were in Mitrovica and everybody else who was evacuated and who was brought to that sports hall from the war-affected area, the JNA evacuated all of you and took you to Croatia; is that right? And nobody was mistreated, tortured, or nobody got killed; is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it was. The convoy that came to Mitrovica, to the sports hall, was brought with representatives of the European Community, the people in white. We managed to join the convoy and to get out. It was not the JNA that evacuated us from the sports hall in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, and who brought you to that sports hall from which you were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were brought to the sports hall by bus from the prison at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these JNA vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were just buses, coaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In whose vehicles were you transported from the final assembly point via Bosnia to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were transported in buses. Whose they were or which buses they were that came from Vukovar, I don't know who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume they did not belong to the European Union, or the European Community at the time, but that it had been organised by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness C-1164, could you please tell Their Honours a few more things by way of clarification. On page 3 of your statement, which is paragraph 8 - it is the third paragraph on that page - during your testimony yesterday you already spoke about the people who were from your town, who you knew by sight, and within that group there were persons who looked scary, who were dirty and who were wearing beards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at the last two sentences of that paragraph. You spent a time in a house. You mentioned the name of the man - I don't have to repeat it - and you say that "We stayed in their house for several hours. We were guarded by two or three young men in JNA uniforms." So I would like to ask you about this expression "we were looked after, or guarded." Did these young men protect you from these people who had a scary appearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They all belonged to the same group. They were not protecting us from them. We couldn't go out. So they were in fact guards who were guarding outside the door of that house. I don't think that they were protecting us from anyone. They were just there so that we couldn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look, please, at page 4, paragraph 12. This is a long paragraph, third in the B/C/S version, where you said that for a time you were in the basement. Then again you mention two names - I don't wish to mention them here - and then they took you from that basement towards the Velepromet factory. And then towards the end you say that you were in a Serb house next to the railway tracks, not far from the factory. You also mention the name of the owner. "There were two women already in that house. Each of them had two children. There were some other people. There was a total of us, 14. It was a private house. I remember that some came from a certain family." You mentioned the name of the family. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "The soldiers brought us food once a day." And then again you use the term "cuvati," which could mean protect or guarded, by a Serb woman. So who did she guard you from or protect you from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was there to check on us and not to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then we have page 5, paragraph 14. Again you use similar terms when describing the bus that took you to Sid in a military vehicle. "We got off the bus," and then you say in the middle of that paragraph, "That was the first time that we saw regular JNA soldiers for the first time." Is that right, that it was only then that you saw JNA soldiers for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was saying that, I meant officers of the JNA. All these others were members of the Territorial Defence, reservists, all these locals of ours in Vukovar wearing uniforms of the then-Yugoslav People's Army. This was the first time that we saw JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, that is not the way you put it. It says here, and I quote, "It was the first time I actually met regular JNA officers." But very well, you've explained that now. Then later on you said, "On the stage, there were several young soldiers who were guarding us or protecting us." Again, they were protecting you so that no one could endanger you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not protecting us so that no one would hurt us. They were there to keep a check on us. They were young soldiers, and it was their duty to check on this hall where we were all staying. There were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to suggest anything to you, I'm just using your words. Because you used the same expression on page 7, second paragraph. When you arrived in the sports hall, again you were looked after by women in uniform, or guarded or protected. This is page 7, paragraph 22. "The women guards never hurt us and they didn't take us to any kind of interrogation during our stay in Sremska Mitrovica." Again you use the words "cuvati" and that no one mistreated you there. Doesn't that mean, after all, that they were in a sense protecting you from physical abuse and mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not in the sense of protection. We were detained there and these were people who were keeping check on the people detained. They were prison guards, looking after prisoners or guarding prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, the last two paragraphs of your statement. You say that you were taken from Sremska Mitrovica. There was a convoy of 1.000 people. And then in the last paragraph, paragraph 26, you said that when you left Sremska Mitrovica -- I know where Sremska Mitrovica is, and I know where the border with Bosnia is. You say that you drove the whole day. Were you secured by the army or the police? I don't know. You were there. Was the convoy escorted by the army or the police up until the Bosnian border and to the spot where you were exchanged? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no answer. First of all, whether it was all day, as I already said, all of us had by then lost all sense of time, what day it was. We didn't even know what season it was. All we cared about was to join the convoy because we were -- we had been alone in Mitrovica, that is, our group. We were not registered. And our main aim was to join this larger group of people and move on. We didn't know where we were going. Whether someone was escorting the convoy, securing the convoy, I can't tell you. What I did see was the men in white.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand all the difficulties you went through, but you were riding in buses. I'm asking whether you saw through the windows any troops or the police securing this convoy and escorting it through much of Serbia to Bosnia, where you were exchanged. It is impossible for such a large convoy not to be escorted so as to secure the safety of such a large number of people. So did you see any escort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone securing the convoy of which we were a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would only like to clarify one matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Milosevic asked you during his cross-examination why your father had grenades in the house, and I would -- you said you would not know that. Do you know whether in Eastern Slavonia grenades and other explosives are used for fishing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did your father occasionally go fishing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1164 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1164, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. Would you just wait until they pull the blinds down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with some administrative matters. Sorry, no, we'll stay in open session just for one moment, please. Tomorrow we are sitting between 9.00 and 12.00, as we've already announced. Also, Judge Robinson has a hospital appointment, and therefore Judge Kwon and I will sit under the appropriate Rule. Judge Robinson, if it's possible, will return, of course. And there is a matter I want to deal with in private session, while we're on to these.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I apologise. May the next witness, David Harland, be brought in. And while he's coming in, may I make the obvious point to which we've also -- which we've also addressed in a filing, that the Prosecution is obviously concerned about the degree to which it's inevitably losing witnesses because of the passage of time -- that is, losing witnesses it won't have the time to call. With this witness, I will attempt to get the essence of his evidence in the shortest possible time. To begin with, I'll only produce one of the two volumes of exhibits and then we'll defer the position about the other one until a little later in proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should say -- I should have said perhaps earlier that Monday's witness is a witness who has to start on Monday, as far as I am aware, and that position seems unlikely to change. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the next witness, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. The next witness is C-028, I think you'll find. That witness is a witness I would very much like to conclude tomorrow. There would then be another witness who will be postponed in order that Monday's witness can start on Monday. But we are very pressed for time and perhaps we can review the position in one of the breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, if the witness would take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this witness there is a first volume of exhibits in 24 tabs, and if we can simply focus on that to begin with. We'll address the position about the other volume a little later. Yes, may the usher have the volume to display on the overhead projector as this hasn't been Sanctioned, I'm afraid. And may the witness have his own volume for ease and speed of reference. Usher, that one can go straight to the -- one can go straight to the witness and -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour will have a summary of this witness's potential evidence in 27 pages. You'll see a number of passages are in italics, and I'm not intending to lead those and I may indeed delete other passages as well in the interest of saving time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: David John Harland. Excuse me, could I say my -- the headset is very squeaky. That's normal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No, when you're listening. Put it on. That's electronic interference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we get this dealt with. Yes, we'll get a technician. Well, let's try, first of all, with another pair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this sound any better?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Not much, no. No, it's quite interfered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps try the other microphone, in case that makes a difference. Usher, the other microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome makes the obvious point: He doesn't need them with me and we can sort it out over the break. I think you'll find I'll be speaking to you in English, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need the technology after all. We'll go back and do it the old-fashioned way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: David John Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as United Nations civil affairs and political affairs officer in Sarajevo - we needn't trouble with all the detail of your movements - did you serve in Sarajevo from 1993 and until 1999, being based for a time in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That made you, I think, the longest serving UN -- senior UN official in Sarajevo. And included in your tasks was a reporting duty. The Chamber is pretty familiar with reporting duties. Yours was, what, to prepare a weekly report?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, there was a regular weekly report which described and analysed the political situation and also there were reports written after almost daily meetings, either with the Pale leadership or with the Sarajevo leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you say "the leadership," as you say in your summary and statement, this is the top-level of leadership, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, to name three?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, also Babic, Gvero, Milovanovic and Karadzic's adviser, Zametica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your meetings at Pale or the Lukavica barracks in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: In Lukavica or in Pale, yes, with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the usher be good enough to help us getting the Sarajevo map - I shan't take time - onto an easel so that we can refer to it if necessary. We'll come to that later and move straight on to paragraph -- page 6, ethnic cleansing. And may we please go to your documents which are in an exhibit which will be given a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 546.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have two binders?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that we just deal with first binder now, reserving the position as to what we do with the second binder as we see how time passes. 546, was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position, Mr. Harland, I think is this, that the documents in Exhibit 546 are some of the various documents and reports that you prepared which you have reviewed generally and which you are happy to present an overall view of your position at the time.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are just using these reports to trigger by odd paragraphs within them particular events and recollections; correct?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we go straight away to tab 2 in this, which we find is a report of the 15th of July - and I'd simply ask the usher to be good enough to try and follow the directions and to display the relevant part - this is your report of the 15th of July. If we go to page 5 of it -- the numbering may have been axed off. I hope it's there. Under the title "Bosnian Serbs," we see this entry: "Meeting with the new Bosnian commander Briquemont and with Andreev, Karadzic made it clear that his first priority was to get the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government in Sarajevo to come to the negotiating table and to start discussing the partition Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. map. Although Srpska has supported exchanges of population, Karadzic emphasised that Serbs recognise right of people of different ethnic background to remain or return to homes in territory allocated to a different community should they so wish. "Karadzic appeared confident that BH would soon be forced to negotiate, Serb military efforts seem to be aimed at getting the BH to the table and at securing as much as territory as possible for anticipated negotiations." Comment on that as a general tactic?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders emphasised to us that their principal goal was to force the Bosnian government to -- to negotiate peace -- a peace agreement on terms that would be acceptable to them and that the reason they were shelling Sarajevo, for example, which I think was what we were protesting about that day, was to -- to apply pressure on the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How, if at all, did this sort of response fit with any justification that could be raised for ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Karadzic generally blamed ethnic cleansing on the international community for not having established any legal mechanism to allow people to exchange their homes and to move into the -- the cantons into which their nationality would be dominant. He felt it would be an inevitable outcome of the international community's failure to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn to tab 3, your report of the 5th of August of 1993, the first page, and right at the bottom where we see this paragraph and then over to the next page. "Karadzic appeared relaxed, confident, and cooperative. He presented proposals on Serb withdrawal from Mount Igman and on the establishment of safe routes in and out of Sarajevo" and is that oil cooperation for the restoration or is that on "cooperation for the restoration of utilities. He indicated that these Serb initiatives would encourage Izetbegovic to join the talks and would remove any suggestion of the use of airstrikes. He proposed that Serb forces withdraw from Mount Bjelaznica and Mount Igman as demanded by Izetbegovic as a precondition for joining the talks in Geneva. Indicated that the Serb offensive in the area was not an attempt to annex those territories to the Republika Srpska but simply part of a military operation intended to deprive BH forces of artillery positions which endangered Serb-controlled areas surrounding Sarajevo. He said that Serb forces would be willing to withdraw so long as UNPROFOR would ensure that BH forces did not re-occupy the area." Your comments on this, please.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, most obviously, of course, it's another example of the -- the Serb modulating their military effort and modulating the amount of terror, that is, the amount of humanitarian difficulty placed on the population of Sarajevo, to -- in the context of a -- for political objectives, that is, of getting the Muslims to negotiate, or in terms of deterring any NATO military attack on them. Our sense was they -- there was, as it were, a spigot of terror which they would open or close according to how much pressure was on them from the international community or what political concessions they hoped to get from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any question of testing NATO's probable reaction? Was there any element of, as I think you called it, cat and mouse?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, there was. NATO had made a number of declarations, and the -- the one in the context of the Mount Igman one was the firmest so far, an indication that they might use NATO air attacks to end the siege of -- of Sarajevo. And this was an example of the Serbs approaching us and saying that they would be willing to make some concessions, such as withdrawing from one Igman-Bijelasnica, it's an area around Sarajevo, and they would be willing to improve the humanitarian situation in Sarajevo if the threat of airstrikes were taken away and if the Bosnian Muslim party would join them in -- in peace talks for a final settlement to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The comparative military activity in the years 1993, 1994, and 1995, please.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: 1993 was the most militarily active of those years. There was a conflict both between the Bosnian government, that is, the Muslims and the Serbs, and between the Bosnian government and the Croats. 1994 was relatively quiet throughout most of the year. And then 1995 saw a sharp deterioration again right up till the end of the war in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Roughly how many shells a day were landing in Sarajevo over that period?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Approximately 1.000, though there were significant lulls during the -- the period of the 1994 cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 17, tab 4 of Exhibit 2 -- 546. Rather than return to an exhibit, and to save time, just look first, please, at the very first page of this, the second starred entry, where in your report of the 31st of November -- I beg your pardon, the 3rd of November, is it? The 3rd of November of 1993, you note that unlike the BH side, the Serbs seem to be directionless. Political leader Karadzic is blocked by Serbia and by the international community at large. Mladic is frustrated and becoming increasingly bellicose. The Serb army has been pounding Sarajevo and Gorazde. Any comments on that before I turn to page 6?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I would just say that our -- this is an assessment drawn from the Bosnian Serbs themselves. They felt, and our military experts tended to agree, that they could have prosecuted the war more vigorously. They could probably even have forced the surrender of Sarajevo, we felt, but they had political reasons not to do that and they often referred to pressure from Milosevic in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we go, then, to page 6 of this same report. One of five paragraphs to read here. Infrequently will I read so much from one of these documents. It's usually much smaller entries. So under Bosnian Serbs -- and the interpreters will tell me if I'm going too fast; I have the headsets on. "The Bosnian Serbs are politically frustrated and increasingly volatile. The pressure on them -- especially from Milosevic -- is intense and a major eruption is possible in the near future. "The Serbs invested heavily in the Owen-Stoltenberg peace package brokered in Geneva. Since the collapse of that package, the Serbs have been less certain and less unified in their political strategy. "Karadzic, acknowledging pressure from Serbia and from the international community at large, appears reluctant to use the Serb war machine to force a settlement." Missing the next paragraph. "Perhaps in an effort to regain centre stage, Mladic has been very vocal recently. One issue which he is following and on which he is striking a strong posture is that of the 22 Serb POWs held in the Gorazde pocket. In a meeting with the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff recently he threatened, among other things, to kill everyone in the Eastern enclaves (except for the children) unless the POWs were not returned by the 10th of November. "Mladic's insistence about the Gorazde POWs (one of whom is the son of one of his senior colleagues) is causing a number of problems for UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR, Mladic feels, could be doing more to secure the POWs' release. Perhaps as a result, Mladic personally held up a French re-supply convoy in Sokolac recently. He also ordered the impounding of two UNPROFOR helicopters returning from Srebrenica. These were released only after intervention from Owen, Stoltenberg, Milosevic, and Karadzic." And then finally, over on page 7, the top paragraph: "The Serbs have been militarily more active than usual recently. They've not been trying to take territory, but their artillery has been busy. Sarajevo and Gorazde have both been under heavy bombardment in the past week. In response to BH mortar fire, the Old Town of Sarajevo received almost 500 shells in a one-hour period on the 27th of October. The Old Town, which has the highest percentage of Muslims of any Sarajevo area, is densely populated." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Any further comment beyond the entries themselves, and how the accused Milosevic features in this, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: At this period we were -- we were aware, of course, that the Bosnian Serb establishment spoke with several voices and the voices didn't always agree. Over time, the differences between the civilian leadership with Karadzic at the centre and the military leadership with Mladic at the centre appeared to grow. And here we can see already some intervention from Milosevic with respect to activities by the -- by the Serb military. As time passed, we felt more confident that there was a degree of -- of influence, if not control, from Milosevic over that military element.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we may see more about that, specifically in relation to Mladic later, I think.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just as an -- not as an aside but as something of a parenthetic observation, perhaps, you see a reference there to Mladic being concerned about someone's son. As a matter of interest, did you make an observation, a general observation, about the personal investment of the leadership in this war, generally?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, it often struck us on all three sides how amazingly little any of the leaders were willing to invest or sacrifice. That unlike in, you know, other wars, such as our countries in World War II or their countries, nobody's children - and they all had military-age sons whom they had all squirreled out of the country or who were serving in -- officially in uniform but just doing desk jobs. And in this case I think it might have been General Talic's son - I can't remember now - was a very strange one, when the son of a high leader had actually got anywhere near a front line and had been captured; an extreme rarity which enraged Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 5, please. And tab 5 is your report of the 9th of February of 1994. We know that this was the year generally a little quieter of military activity. Page 2 -- if we can go to page 2 of it. We come to a well-known incident. And it's the mortar bomb landing in Sarajevo's old town at lunchtime on the Friday, with 68 people being killed. And your report on page 2 goes on to say how the ballistics expert confirmed that all the casualties were caused by a single bomb, the round fired from the north-east, from near the confrontation line, not possible to say for certain that it came from Serb positions. The attack was, however, similar to one the day before in which Serb gunners caused 28 casualties when they mortared civilians waiting in line for humanitarian aid. "The massacre was followed by renewed calls from the BH Presidency to bomb Serb gunners surrounding the city." A sympathetic response from the international community is summarised as to both UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, foreign ministers of the EU, and so on. Now, what was the overall effect of this, the first Markale shelling, please?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, the overall effect was a stabilisation of the situation around Sarajevo. The Serbs told us that they wanted to make a number of dramatic concessions on the humanitarian front and on the military front so as to head off the possibility of any possible NATO air attacks. And the cease-fire that resulted lasted through -- well, at least through the summer of 1994 and into the autumn of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see a conclusion from what a ballistics expert said. Was there only the one investigation at that stage, or was there a two-stage or a double investigation?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, there were at least two. And in fact, the -- the initial report -- I was with Krajisnik and Silajdzic and General Rose, the UNPROFOR commander, at the -- negotiating at the airport when the shell landed. There was a very quick initial report which indicated that the shell -- the mortar bomb had probably come from inside the confrontation line, that is, it had come from Bosnian government positions firing against themselves. There was then a -- a fuller investigation or -- in which they determined that that was in error and that the shell had come from an area just north-east of the old town area - about here where I'm pointing to on the map - which could have been either side of the confrontation line. In other words, no final determination could ever definitively be made as to who fired it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure whether His Honour Judge Robinson has sight of the map because of the angle. I don't know if there's an easel upon which the map can be placed. If there is ... Have you got an easel, usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The old town of Sarajevo is here in the valley of Sarajevo. The mortar came from this high ground to the north-east of the old town, and the -- the confrontation line runs roughly where I'm putting the indicator now. And the -- the ballistics experts were aiming -- only able to determine it came from somewhere within that -- that range. So it was a rather unsatisfactory investigation in many ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll get an easel for the second session and we'll deal with matters of map geography then. Tab 6, please. Did you tell us, I think, a complete cease-fire following Markale was agreed for the 10th of February?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 6 is your report for the 17th of February. Page 3 of that, just over halfway down, a record of the humanitarian situation being -- in Sarajevo being relatively good. Water, electricity, and gas still limited, food flowing in well, lack of adequate supplies of especially gas is important because Sarajevo is in the grip of the coldest weather this winter. Night-time temperatures falling to below minus 20 degrees centigrade and the government claiming that the valves on the gas supply lines turned off by the Serbs, who deny this and say the problem originated in Serbia. Can you give an observation about gas supplies generally and deal with it perhaps comprehensively here?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: All right. Well, as the Judges probably know, gas for Bosnia-Herzegovina comes along a pipeline from Russia. It passes from Russia to Hungary to Serbia, across the border into Bosnia, I think at Zvornik, then down through Kladanj, then Olovo and into Sarajevo. Now, it could be cut off or pressure could be reduced at several points, and this would induce great suffering for particularly the old people of Sarajevo because they had no heating. And often people died when there was no gas, the vulnerable. So we made a large effort to try and keep it on. The Serbs -- Bosnian Serbs in particular, I should say, often cut off the gas or reduced its pressure in order to apply political pressure to the Bosnian Muslims to -- to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The same report, now can we go to page 6, please, top paragraph. "The threat of NATO airstrikes has made the Serbs more cooperative than usual. The Serb policy was summed up by the Assembly president Krajisnik, who stated, 'We will do everything to avoid airstrikes except capitulate." A word or two about that, relating it to the Markale incident if appropriate.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, Krajisnik was just one of many who very directly stated the dilemma as they saw it. They wanted to put as much pressure on the Bosnian Muslims as possible by making life as difficult for them as possible, by taking as much territory as possible, but not pushing the situation so far that it would bring about a NATO military intervention of any sort. So they sought to modulate their military and humanitarian pressure according to the -- the likelihood as they perceived it of a -- of a NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 7, please, your report of the 1st of March of 1994, page -- the first page, which is actually page 2 at the bottom. And under "Sarajevo," the third paragraph reads: "The Serbs have been caught moving heavy weapons inside the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. In the most serious incident, seven T-55 tanks are seen in the Sarajevo suburb of Ilidza." And then if we turn over to page 5, please, under "Bosnian Serbs," the fourth paragraph and fifth paragraph: "Serb leader Karadzic has approved an extension of freedom of movement: bus routes, Zenica-Sarajevo and Pale-Sarajevo are to be opened; some pedestrian traffic is to be allowed between downtown Sarajevo and neighbouring Grabovica. BSA Chief of Staff Milovanovic stated on the 27th of February, however, that the Serb military would knot not allow the United Nations unrestricted freedom of movement over Serb territory. "Milovanovic stated that his forces would block UN convoys, regardless of the joint declaration signed by Srpska President Karadzic on the 18th of November, 1993 and even at the risk of NATO airstrikes. He added that Serbs would not allow the UN or anyone else to use the Bratsvo-Jedinstvo bridge linking Serb-held districts of Sarajevo to the main downtown area." Now, your comment about this. We've heard a little bit about the exclusion zone already. And what about the tanks? Where were they going?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe those tank -- I believe those tanks were on their way to participate in the attack on armed guards that was about to happen. I must say it was a relatively small incident. As I hear you read it, the thing that strikes me here is that it was one of an increasing number of statements by the Bosnian Serb military that they didn't care what the Bosnian Serb civilian leadership said. Here we have General Milovanovic stating that whatever Karadzic has done, he is going to take certain actions, and that grew over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, me may be asking you later to give some more overview answers about the influence and power of one over the other. But let's move on in the developing picture of which you're giving an overview to tab 7, please, your -- I beg your pardon, tab 8, your report of the 9th of March. We can see on the first page, the first line under "Highlight," says "Peace appears to be breaking out in much of Bosnia." And then on the second page, under "Sarajevo," "Most days there are fewer than 5 heavy weapons violations in the exclusion zone. Civilian casualties mainly from sniping average fewer than one per day. Some small-arms fire is still heard, however, particularly where the confrontation line runs through the downtown area, Grbavica-Jewish cemetery." We'll perhaps pick that detail up for the judges later. Anything else you want to say about the tone of optimism that now is to be found in your report?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, nothing, except to say that this was a very encouraging time for us all. The Muslim-Croat war had come to an end under American pressure, and the Serb -- the Serb concessions after the NATO threats, after the Markale attack, had also stabilised the Muslim-Serb confrontation line. So there was a -- a substantial relief of the humanitarian situation during -- during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, then, let's go to tab 9, the 16th of April. We can see on the second page, page 2, headed "Gorazde crisis," a summary of events there. And if we go down to -- towards the bottom of the page, this: "Gorazde had been reasonably quiet for several days following a second use of NATO air power. "Late Monday morning, artillery rounds began landing in the centre of Gorazde town. At 11.45 a demonstration of close air support was made, and at 12.25 General Mladic was verbally warned that air power would be used if the shelling did not stop immediately. NATO jets made further low passes over the area, but shelling continued. Russian envoy Churkin then spoke to Serbian President Milosevic who, in his presence, called Dr. Karadzic and told him that the firing must stop. At 14.19, following further low passes by NATO aircraft, two US F-18 jets struck at a tank and two armoured personnel carriers. All three vehicles are believed to have been destroyed." If we can turn over to page 4, halfway down the page: "On Thursday, the 14th of April, 1994 Serbian President Milosevic was quoted in the Belgrade daily Politika as `expressing his conviction that the Serb side would accept new negotiations without prejudice to the conditions of a general cessation of hostilities.'" And two paragraphs on, under "Comment," "It appears that Serbian President Milosevic is attempting to appeal to the best interests of Bosnian Serbs, pointing out that a major conflict with NATO is in nobody's interests except Sarajevo's. Pale, however, appears defiant and ready to take the risk that NATO will not intervene to defend the designated area." I hope we've extracted enough from this substantial report to enable you to give some comments and in particular your comments on where you think the accused Milosevic fits into this part of the narrative.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. In April of 1994, the Serbs decided to attack Gorazde. The UNPROFOR attempted to stabilise the situation, as did other members of the international community, including Russian envoy Churkin. We had meetings -- constant meetings, both in Pale and in Belgrade. Our strong impression, as stated to us by the Pale leadership, was that they wanted to continue their -- their attack on -- on Gorazde as vigorously as possible. They also relayed to us their concern that Milosevic was trying to persuade them to call it off, because he was -- he was worried about possible NATO intervention in the war, which they seemed less concerned about at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was Karadzic's response, I think when General Rose asserted that guns were still firing despite Karadzic saying they weren't? If you can remember.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: There was a -- there was a very high level of frustration, most pointedly when Mr. Churkin walked out of the talks altogether and, in fact, never returned, after he said he had never heard so many lies. But despite those difficulties, in fact, Mr. Milosevic, as they told us, the Bosnian Serbs told us, had prevailed on the Serb military to pull back, and an agreement was made and stabilised the situation in -- around Gorazde, and it was stabilised without significant loss of life. So despite the frustrations of Mr. Churkin and others, the international interventions and the work with Milosevic had -- had helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember one meeting where Krajisnik was present and where he left the room from time to time to speak to others? And if so, to which others did he speak, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there is -- at the Hotel Panorama, where these meetings took place, there is a small meeting room -- sorry, a small telephone booth room off the main conference room, and Krajisnik would go into that room. He went in several times and said, "I've spoken to Milosevic," or, "I've spoken to Mladic." Mladic was not very far away, but he was directing Serb forces around Gorazde, so he wasn't at the meeting. So Krajisnik was clearly in a -- a state of some -- some agitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on now then, please, to tab 10, 15th of October of 1993. So -- is that correct? We've changed a year back and we're on a different topic; sniping and shelling and the campaign generally. You've said something already about whether this was a focussed campaign or whether it had a different objective. But let's look at this report, first page, paragraph 3: "General Briquemont stated that he had seen no evidence of it, but that he noticed that Serb shelling of civilian areas in Sarajevo was increasing. He insisted that this has no military value and causes political damage to the Serbs. Dr. Karadzic stated that he had given orders for shelling and sniping to stop. He said Muslim shelling and sniping was a major problem and that he might 'be forced to take the Muslim part of Sarajevo if the sniping does not stop.'" Can we then look immediately to tab 11, which is the, I think, 16th of October. There may be an error in the initial dating of this document. And if we go to the last page of it, unnumbered pages, but the first asterisked paragraph. We can see here Karadzic claiming to have given written orders halting sniping and shelling in Sarajevo. Briquemont pointing out that sniping and shelling are continuing. Karadzic stating this was the action of rogue individuals, that he would take further action to curb it if the Muslim side would do the same. Your general comment, please, about complaints and protests being made about shelling and sniping and the general response to the Bosnian Serbs and whether you accepted their response.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I should say this is a fairly typical week. This doesn't -- in fact, I have no particular memory of this week as opposed to others, but it was certainly a normal pattern. And the first thing to note is that the pattern of shelling was very distressing to the military commanders in UNPROFOR who were generally NATO military officers. One of the normal tactical principles of artillery bombardment, of course, is concentration of fire. You concentrate fire in order to clear ground or suppress enemy fire in order to take it or something. Whereas, the pattern of artillery fire around Sarajevo was precisely the opposite; it was a dispersion of fire. Shells would be dropped apparently randomly across the densely populated civilian areas of the city in a way that would cause a small number of casualties in a large number of places. We assumed that this was to keep the general level of terror high and to forestall any dramatic events around which an international response would coalesce. With respect to your second question about the chain of command, yes. Whenever we would prevail upon the Bosnian Serbs to -- to restrain themselves or to issue orders, they would complain that they had only limited control over the snipers and the artillerymen involved. However, we noted that when they passed orders which they wanted implemented, as opposed to ones which they were doing -- they were issuing at our behest, they found them quite -- quite easy to implement. So we felt that the Serbs were -- were dissembling. They were exaggerating their problems of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look now at tab 12, which is an agreement of the 14th of August of 1994, signed by General Karavelic for the BiH army and by General Dragomir Milosevic for the VRS, we find an agreement which includes, under the undertakings, that they shall within 24 hours issue publicly orders which explicitly forbid sniping activities against military personnel, civilians, and UN personnel. What does their signing up to that show to you?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, yes. The most significant thing about this agreement from our point of view was that sniping did stop almost entirely for the at least six-week period after it. And what it seemed to show to us was that both sides, which always claimed that they had no control over snipers, when they wanted to, could in fact stop sniping almost completely relatively easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're on page 12, in paragraphs 30 and following of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 31. Any references to uncontrolled paramilitaries? You may have told us about this expressly, but if not, just fill it in. Was the phrase "uncontrolled paramilitaries" ever referred to, and what view did you take of that?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not at the moment. Just generally.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The Serbs in particular often said that they were unable to restrain or limit restrictions on humanitarian aid or limit shelling or sniping because those actions might be taken by some paramilitary groups, often from Serbia, over which they said they had no command and control. And, for example, there is a -- a little dent in the confrontation line at a place called Nedzarici, where I'm pointing to on the map, where there was said to be a -- a unit of Chetnik irregulars under the command of a certain Aleksic. And they -- it was right near the main road and they would often shoot at people on the main road. And when we protested it, they would say, "Unfortunately, these are people who are not part of our chain of command."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But your view about that, in due course, was?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Our view was that when they had a positive will to pass an order, they were able to implement that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your description of the campaign -- terrorising campaign, or however you would summarise it, and its objectives in relation to signing peace agreements, was that ever expressly acknowledged by any of the Pale leadership?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And in these documents and in many others, we would come back with quotes from Karadzic and Krajisnik and Koljevic and Mladic and others, saying, "We will continue to do these things until Izetbegovic accepts the Owen-Stoltenberg peace plan," for example. I remember them being very vigorous about we will only turn on the -- the electricity or give them gas or allow food in if they will make further concessions on one of the later peace plans. No, it was a common theme, and they didn't even try to hide it from us, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if your interpretation is correct and if the things that were said to you were correct, then what connection, in your judgement, was there between what was happening in Sarajevo and population movements being enforced elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Certainly Dr. Karadzic openly said - and so did Dr. Plavsic, in particular - that the basic goal of the basic Serb war aim was to redistribute the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that the Serbs would be left in control of a -- a single continuous block of territory embracing the whole of the border with Montenegro and Serbia and also including all of the traditionally Serb-inhabited areas. And due to an historical accident, this required the removal of very large numbers of Bosnian Muslims because Bosnian Muslims were the majority population along the Drina River Valley in North-Eastern Bosnia, adjacent to Serbia. So they were quite open that the purpose of these -- of the war and the purpose of the pressure they were applying was to extract from the Bosnian government an acceptance of this redistribution of the populations, this ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in your judgement, did that pressure include what was being done at Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. Not only in my judgement, but as they directly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think paragraph 36: UNPROFOR reached a conclusion by a sampling of Bosnian households and other things that defence of the city was untenable without a flow of water and gas, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It -- the supply of that was in fact dependent on cooperation of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is back to your spigot point?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo was completely sounded. By agreement with the Serbs, in 1992 UNPROFOR had taken control of Sarajevo airport, which had been Serb controlled, and the Bosnian Muslims later dug a tunnel under that, giving them access to the main block of their territory. So there was a tiny supply line of their own, more or less tolerated by the -- the Serbs. Karadzic even said he tolerated it. But in general, the city relied for water, food, electricity, gas, and almost everything else on the -- the -- on the Serbs to let those things through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 13, page 2 in your report of the 10th of December of 1994. Coming to the end of that year. "This office spoke with the Chief of Staff, General Brinkman, this morning, and he made the obvious point that it is no longer particularly useful to protest individual incidents of this nature, as we are not dealing with random incidents, we are dealing with an organised campaign. The incidents will stop when the campaign of obstruction and harassment stops." A small point. How does that fit in with the account you've just given us or is it reflective of it?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Very much. Because the -- the Serbs knew or felt - and they told us that they felt - that the Bosnian Muslims would not sign a peace agreement unless there was substantial pressure on them. The Serbs rightly understood that we were facilitating the entry of humanitarian goods into Sarajevo and so we were in some sense acting contrary to their war aims. And when they grew particularly frustrated at the lack of political progress, as well as directing their fire at the Bosnian Muslims, they would very strongly obstruct our own efforts to bring humanitarian relief to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 14 of the summary, the reference to Exhibit number 16 I'll tidy up by the second session. I'll move straight to tab 14, please, page 3, and paragraph 2, of this report of the 24th of June of 1995. We can see on page 3, just a third of the way down, that "On Sunday, the 18th of June, UNPROFOR withdrew from all of the weapons collections points around Sarajevo, maintaining that the heavy weapons total exclusion zone, established in February 1994, is in existence but that it was not -- no longer possible to support it with troops on the ground. The Serbs are believed to have about 500 heavy weapons within 20 kilometres of Sarajevo. The Bosnians are believed to have about 100 to 150, and it seem that is most of these weapons are now being deployed for action." And then at the foot of that page: Shelling. Serb gunners have killed a large number of Bosnian civilians this week, shelling water lines and marketplaces. Seven people were killed and 12 injured when queuing for water in Dobrinja on Sunday, the 18th of June. On Wednesday, the 21st, six people were killed and 15 injured in another attack on a Dobrinja water line. The same day, five people were injured when a shell hit the Ciglane outdoor market. The next day, 22nd of June, one more person killed and five injured, improvised rocket at the TV building. This is a reflection of what?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Several things. First, the -- the weapons collection points, which were established under the threat of NATO air attacks under the first Markale attack, were areas in Serb territory where the Serbs had agreed to concentrate their weapons so that we could send some monitors there. As the situation degenerated, we wanted to withdraw our monitors so there would be no hostages available to be taken if we had to call on NATO air attacks. And they also wanted to take weapons out of those areas so they could resume the -- their campaign against the -- basically the civilian population of Sarajevo in order to force the government to make a political accommodation with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And this was all part of the deteriorating situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber would be good enough to go to tab -- well, tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is your report for the 3rd of June. If we could go and look at page 2, paragraph 5. And it's paragraphs 40 and 41 of the -- of the summary. On paragraph -- on page 2, paragraph 5 we see this: "On Friday, the International Committee of the Red Cross had a meeting with Koljevic in Pale pledging that UN personnel held in detention --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please read slower, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Held in detention by the Bosnian Serb army would be released unconditionally as a gesture of goodwill. 120 hostages were indeed released and transported to Serbia, but the Bosnian Serbs still kept about 200 of them. Apparently the release was effected due to pressure by Milosevic on Karadzic and was fairly well coordinated by the military and the security services." Can you -- thank you very much. Can you summarise that for us, focussing on the accused Milosevic's role in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then we must break after that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. Well, some hostages had been taken by the Bosnian Serbs after we had authorised some air attacks by NATO on them. The Bosnian Serbs had been inclined to escalate this confrontation. They told us rather directly that they were under pressure from Mr. Milosevic to -- to be cooperative, to release the hostages or at least to hand them over to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who would then release them. And this was done, and our released hostages reported that the -- the operation had gone very smoothly, as between the Bosnian Serb hostage-takers and the Serbian security personnel who had taken some of the hostages back to safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Harland, could you please remember in this and any other adjournments not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I've been asked to leave -- by the interpreters to leave a pause between question and answer, my fault, not yours. But if you can help with that, I'd be very grateful. Page 14 of the summary, paragraph 43. In the summer of 1995, Mr. Harland, did you see a new type of bomb? Tell us about it briefly.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. There were a small -- there were a small number of bombs. I saw one from my window in the PTT building in June. It was a -- they were large relatively slow-moving -- slower moving than mortar shells, because you could see them as they were airborne -- coming from a northerly direction. And the one I -- the one I saw hit the television building, the RTV building, which was close to my PTT engineering location. It made a very loud detonation and sent up a plume of white -- of white smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they appear to have any ability to be aimed or focussed on where they were landing?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Judging from their trajectory, it was a parabolic trajectory, so it was not particularly -- it was an area weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This incident was, I think, covered in the last exhibit we may have looked at but is more particularly covered at tab 15, your report of the 2nd of July of 1995. I think we'll find that on page 2, but I'll look at a few entries there for your comment. On the top of page 2: "Early in the week, Serb forces counter-attacked in Cemerska heights to the north of the city and on the eastern slopes of Igman. In both areas they seem to have pushed the Bosnians back. On Wednesday, the Bosnians attempted another attack out of the city. The main attack came from the western part of the town, focussed on Serb-held Nedzarici." The next paragraph but one: "Both sides seem to see the unfolding battle as a critical moment in the war. Serb officials told the civil affairs during the week that they believe the outcome of this battle will decide the outcome of the war. They seem reasonably confident they will contain the Bosnian offensive, and have even said they will launch punitive counter-attacks against the urban area." The bottom of the page, the reference to this type of weapon that we've just touched on: "Improvised rockets fired at the Alipasno area. One struck the RTV building, home to much of the international press corps, killing one person, injuring more than 30 others, including several foreign correspondents. The same day, four people killed when a similar weapon hit a nearby apartment building, destroying apartments on three floors. UNPROFOR condemned the use of what it called `highly inaccurate indiscriminate, highly destructive weapons of terror.'" And finally -- or nearly finally, over the page, the top of the page: "Sniper activity has spread to a number of areas usually considered safe. On Sunday, a 16-year-old boy killed while riding his bicycle near UNPROFOR headquarters. Sniping spread to the old town." Then going on two pages to page 5, three-quarters of the way down under the heading: "UNHCR brings convoy over Igman for the first time without informing the Serbs". Second paragraph, "It was the first time since the war began that a convoy had been brought into Sarajevo area without the express consent of the Serbs. Seven trucks," and so on. Your comment generally on what was happening at this time. We've already dealt with the new type of weapon.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: There was a sense in UNPROFOR that the Serbs had changed tactics, that is, since 19 -- since the autumn of 1992, with the fall of Jajce, the Serbs had basically been during our period in a -- in a defensive posture. They held most of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 70 per cent of it, and they -- they used their military capacity not to take more territory in general, but just to inflict a certain level of terror and hardship on their enemies in order to induce their enemies to -- to accept the terms of a peace agreement that would be generous to the -- to the Serbs. Now, the assumption of this defensive posture they -- they adopted was that time was on their side. By 1995, however, enough weapons were getting to the Bosnian government and the relations between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Croats had improved to such a degree that there was a real military threat from the Bosnian government for the first time, and of course the Bosnian government actually had a numerical advantage in -- in troop strength over the Serbs, and the Serbs became anxious of that. The Serbs were also aware that the government of Croatia was vastly more powerful than the Croatian Serb party and that the government of Croatia was preparing to destroy the Croatian Serb party. Now, the Serbs therefore decided, as they told us, that they had to quickly resolve the situation in Bosnia, and one of the ways in which they sought to do that was to reduce the eastern enclaves and the threat from Sarajevo in order to be able to move troops west to the -- to the main front, where the -- where the Croats were -- were gathering. And these events which are being described in this report are all part of that and part of a fairly successful reaction by them to a Bosnian attempt to break out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll pass over tab 17 directly to tab 18. Sorry, I didn't leave a gap. I should have done. Your report of the 8th of July, page 2 of it, under "Attacks on civilians." "Sniping and mortaring are still at a reasonably high level. This seems to have no particular military value but contributes to a general atmosphere of terror in the city. Almost no civilians now use the city's main east-west thoroughfare ('Sniper Alley') -- so much so that snipers who used to work that area now seem to have relocated. Sporadic, almost random, bombardment of the city continues, and the Ministry of Health reported 39 civilian deaths and 190 wounded this week, most of them from mortars." The Chamber is already acquainted with the road that amounts to Sniper Alley, but perhaps you'd just point it out very rapidly now that the map is on an easel.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo, of course, is in the floor of a valley. The Serbs were on the hills on either side, the Muslims were at the bottom. The Serbs controlled a part of the downtown area, Grbavica, here, which fronts onto this main road which we called Sniper Alley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say the Muslims were at the bottom. You mean they were at the bottom of the valley or --

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: They were at the bottom of the valley. That is, the whole valley of Sarajevo, as in other Bosnian cities, was predominantly Muslim, and as in other Bosnian areas, the hills surrounding were predominantly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there was a historical reason for that that you could give if we ever find the time in this trial.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you actually visited a sniper's position yourself, didn't you, sometime in 1995? Give us an indication of what it was like.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was just before this time, I did, with the help of the Russian Battalion, which was stationed in the Serb area of the downtown part of the city. I visited a sniper nest which they had identified which was overlooking Sniper Alley and -- and Marin Dvor. And it was a standard sniper position.
