It was in an apartment building, a small aperture had been made in the outer wall and then sandbagged around it to resist counter-fire. A second aperture had been made in the next wall internal in the house. The sniper had put an armchair and a cigarette stand and a television, in fact, in back, along with a mount for his gun, along which he could line up the two holes and shoot at civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without being at risk of being -- sorry, I didn't leave a gap. Without being at risk of being fired back on because he was firing through two apertures?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Without significant risk. Though there was a lot of sniper-on-sniper activity and they got very good. In fact, snipers, we observed, would move between three or five of these nests in a morning, in a shift, in order to resist -- to avoid counter-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 19, please. The 15th of July, page 4, as it is numbered on the bottom, under the heading "Military situation around Sarajevo..." Second paragraph from the top: "Despite the relative lull, the Serbs continue a sporadic bombardment of the downtown area -- apparently in an effort to terrorise the population, rather than to attain any particular military objective." Yes?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 50 of the summary, on page 17. You've told us in general about the -- the meetings that you had, and in addition to the names you've given, I think Zametica and Buha were others you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were dealing with the Bosnian Serb side, did you get any evidence or indication from them whether they'd been to Serbia or Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. They -- they would often -- Mr. Buha, I think, lived there, Dr. Buha, for quite a long time. And they -- they were often late for meetings in Pale, saying they had just got back from meetings in -- in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which ones of them said that, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: The ones that seemed to spend the most time there, I would say, would be Koljevic, Krajisnik, Zametica. Koljevic -- I think Plavsic spent a lot of time in Novi Sad, I think she said, and then of course she had a problem entering Serbia sometimes. But yes, certain -- I would say Koljevic was the one who spent the most time. General Mladic too would often come back saying he had -- sorry he was late, he had just been coming back from meetings in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your view, paragraph 51, of the Bosnian Serb command and control structure. You've touched on this a bit already in reflecting how they were able to effect decisions when they wanted to. Any particular examples beyond those you've given? Have you touched on the evacuation of Serbs from Gorazde in October 1994?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. There was a very complex operation. You mentioned this morning the concern General Mladic had about the son of his colleague who was one of 22 prisoners of war held by the Muslims in -- in Gorazde. An arrangement for their release was finally made, and it was a very complicated operation, involving humanitarian assistance coming in, people going out, people going to third places, other people independent of the process having to enter. This was all choreographed very effectively by the Serbs; mines were removed, checkpoints were informed. We were actually very favourably impressed by the efficient command and control arrangements of the Bosnian Serb side during this episode in which they clearly wanted to secure the -- the release of this one young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 18 of the summary, paragraph 52. We've already seen the threat by Mladic in tab 4 to everybody being killed in the Eastern enclaves except the children. Was there any occasion where Karadzic said something that you can recollect about the consequences for Muslims on a numeric basis if there was no cooperation with the Serbs? Or what would happen to Muslim towns?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean, he frequently said, "If they don't cooperate we will take more of their towns." And in fact, I remember this one meeting, I remember it most because General Mladic then contradicted him. Karadzic said, "If the Muslims don't do what we want --" and I forget what it was at that meeting -- "we will take up to five of their municipalities. We might trade back two in a final peace settlement, but they've got to know that we are -- we are going to keep making things worse for them" until they agree to the peace settlement that he was pursuing at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, what did you understand that to mean? They would take the towns by removing the Muslims or by -- by killing them or by whatever means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't -- he didn't specify. Our experience, though, of the other towns they had taken showed a fairly standard pattern, I mean, that would imply very -- very dire consequences for the local population. So it was a -- a threat we were obliged to take seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As to the method?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they would militarily secure a place, defeating the -- the Muslim defenders, and then they would disarm them and they would -- there would normally be some killings, even of those who had surrendered. Some of the women from other places had been subjected to abuses, including rape, and there had been large-scale deportations, sometimes from the whole -- the whole town. Like Jajce had been surrounded and taken and the whole city had been deported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what I'm trying to get at is whether you had formed a view as to the policy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We -- we felt that if they took the five towns, their policy would be to ethnically cleanse them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you form a view as to any antagonism between the Pale civilian leadership and Belgrade or between the Pale civilian leadership and the Bosnian Serb military?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, both. And the Pale leadership was -- was quite open about that in -- in many ways. During the attack on Gorazde, for example, after the formal meetings, I stayed behind at the Hotel Panorama. In fact, we weren't allowed to go back, so officially, I suppose, we were hostages. But we stayed behind and I talked with Zametica, Jovan Zametica, and he said that Milosevic was being unhelpful; in other words, Karadzic wanted to continue the offensive on Gorazde and Milosevic was inclined to restrain the Bosnian Serbs, and as he put it to me then and later, he successfully exercised influence over Mladic to -- to stop the attack before they took any of the downtown area or eliminated the pocket completely, which militarily they could probably have done relatively easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As between the Pale civilian and Bosnian Serb leaderships?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I mean, that was a part of it. The Bosnian Serb civilian leadership, they were mumbling to us their frustration in the spring of 1994, though during this case which we are discussing now, Gorazde. But as time went by, they became more and more open, and Karadzic used the word "insubordinate" to describe -- publicly even -- to describe Mladic's behaviour. Milovanovic and Mladic would say, "We aren't taking orders from Karadzic." Sometimes Karadzic, at the beginning of August 1995, even officially I believe, fired Mladic, but Mladic continued in his post with the support of -- of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you form a view - paragraph 55 - of Mladic's connections, if any, to the VJ or to the accused?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there were several levels of it. I mean, first of all, there was a basic level of support from Serbia to the Bosnian Serbs and in particular to the Bosnian Serb military. They, you know, provided them with everything from money to vehicle maintenance and, you know, anti-aircraft systems, and so on. So there was a level of common cause, and the military emphasised that they -- their chain of command really ran to Belgrade. And when I personally had to write the signs for negotiation meetings for General Mladic and the Bosnian Serb delegation, he would cross out the word "Bosnian" and say, "No, no, we are a single Serb delegation. You know, Belgrade is our capital," and so on. And in general, when we had problems with getting the Bosnian Serb civilians to take the appropriate decision, there would often be a delegation would go to Belgrade, as in this Gorazde case we were discussing, and talk with Milosevic, who would be able to bring about the desired outcome with the -- with the Bosnian Serb military. So there was certainly a -- a level of influence. How far it went, we were never completely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before we part from this topic, you've already mentioned the level of support that came from Serbia. And you may want to say something about tanks as well in your reply, because I think you have a view about that. But if there was support in logistics, materiel, equipment, weaponry, or money, continuing after 1992, how does one reconcile that with the tensions that you say there were between the decisions made by the Pale leadership and the view of Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think that -- that is a good question. I think that the -- there was certainly - and the Pale leadership never denied it - a certain basic level of support that allowed them to prosecute the war and the campaigns of ethnic cleansing. And they were proud of -- of the support they got. However, they felt that Mr. Milosevic was an opportunist, rather than a true Serb nationalist. In fact, Dr. Plavsic used to rather loudly complain that she wished that Mr. Milosevic was more like Dr. Tudjman, that is, willing to send in formed units of his own army and willing to provide passports for the citizen -- for the co-nationals in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And they were frustrated that having embarked together on this joint enterprise, Mr. Milosevic seemed to hold their hand at Sarajevo, at Gorazde, at Igman, and in other places, and that he did it through -- through his control in -- or his influence on -- on the military. That was a source of great frustration to the Bosnian Serb civilian leaders I spoke to, and they regularly complained about it to me and to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you form a view at the time about the level of support, including financial support, that was coming from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: At the time -- I'm much clearer in retrospect, but at the time, I must say we were not a hundred per cent sure. There was a mutiny of a part of the Serb army or at least a disturbance, of a part of the Serb army around Banja Luka, in -- it was the time of the Owen Stoltenberg plan, so it was September of 1993. And Mladic moved to Banja Luka to deal with the problem. So when we needed to deal with Mladic, we used to helicopter to Banja Luka, which had previously been off-limits to us. And as we ran into soldiers and junior officers of the Serb army in Banja Luka, it transpired that a lot of this dispute was about pay and their expectation that they were going to be paid from the Yugoslav army or at least from the same sources as the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Something for us, Mr. Harland. Dealing with the relationship as expressed by the Bosnian Serb leadership with Mr. Milosevic, you used this expression, "They were frustrated that having embarked together on this joint enterprise, Mr. Milosevic seemed to have held their hand at Sarajevo, Gorazde, and Igman, and he did it through his control or his influence on the military." Could you clarify what you mean by or what you were told about their having embarked together on a joint enterprise. Can you clarify that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. They would say -- actually, they would call it the "Serbian national project." Whenever we referred to ethnic cleansing or the war or whatever, they would say - particularly Professor Plavsic, Dr. Zametica, Professor Koljevic - that the Serbian national project had been launched with the full understanding of -- of Serbia and that they had got a lot of support and, in fact, Professor Koljevic always said, "We always thought this war would only last a few days and that the -- the JNA," as the army was then called, not the VJ, "the JNA would be able to clean things up very quickly. " And their -- their frustrations had grown over time. And as -- as they articulated it, as the Western pressure in particular on Serbia, on Mr. Milosevic had mounted, they had felt themselves rather as if the rug had been pulled out from underneath them. Of course, they still had all the JNA military equipment, including, we estimated about 300 tanks that had been left by the JNA, by the Yugoslav authorities when they officially left Bosnia and Herzegovina under Western pressure in May of 1992, but the -- the support wasn't as fulsome as they hoped to be able to bring the war to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you also explain more specifically what you meant by "holding their hand." That would suggest an element of -- of restraint, of pulling back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I meant, staying their hand. The Bosnian Serbs told us regularly, at several -- at many levels that they -- they wanted to take Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica and to hold it as a way of tightening the siege on Sarajevo, because that would effectively stop any leakage of material into Sarajevo from -- from this narrow corridor out. They also told us that they had wanted to take Gorazde or at least reduce it just to a tiny population centre, both because they wanted that finally to be a part of Republika Srpska, because it's near the Serbian border, and also because a large amount of troops were required to garrison it and they wanted to take it and Mr. Milosevic, under Western pressure, had persuaded them not to or not to prosecute the offensive so far. And -- and that was true in other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This may be related, and I had intended to ask you at the end of the examination-in-chief: In the earlier part of your testimony, you said that Karadzic, in response to pressure from Serbia and the international community at large, appeared reluctant to use the Serb war machine to force a settlement. And I had intended to ask you to clarify the pressure from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I'm simply reporting what the Bosnian Serbs told us, and they said, Dr. Karadzic in particular, that he might have wanted to do a number of things which he was -- in particular around Sarajevo. He -- they were always considering cutting off the water and -- and other things, and he was talking both with us and with his associates about influence from Serbia to stop that. And this pattern continued all the way through, until after the fall of Srebrenica too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few questions to tidy up on that as you've been covering, one matter of detail. The tanks, so far as you understood, did they need servicing? And if so, where were they serviced?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. We felt that there was -- they certainly needed servicing, and that there were some maintenance facilities available to the Bosnian Serb army in Bosnian Serb-held territory, but there was also movement of them across the border for -- for maintenance purposes. And members of the Bosnian Serb army we would run into would even refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second question: From what you're describing - and this covers what period, post-1992 or ...?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: From my arrival in the spring of 1993 until the end of the war in the late autumn, early winter of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Milosevic staying the hand or holding the hand to the degree he did covers what period?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I should say that our awareness of this came principally from the Bosnian Serbs and so one has to factor in some possible level of disinformation. But we had many Bosnian Serb sources, and they seemed to agree on it. But I would say it grew over time. Mladic -- in their version, the influence of Milosevic over Mladic grew over time and reached its peak in 1995, when Karadzic was so concerned about it that he attempted to dismiss Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That really takes care of my next question: What does this say about the accused's authority or control or influence over Mladic and others? That he had some?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, he clearly had at least influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then this -- of course, the Trial Chamber will in due course have to decide it insofar as it needs to, the level of financial, logistical, materiel support to the Bosnian Serbs, and in particular to the Bosnian Serb army. If that support had been withdrawn earlier and cut off, what would have been the consequences for both Sarajevo and the surrounding areas which, as you've told us, were affected by what was happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, obviously Bosnian Serb domination of the battlefield was largely a function of support from -- from Belgrade. In fact, the -- the Bosnian Serbs were outnumbered by their enemies. They were substantially outnumbered by the Bosnian Muslims alone, but they had provided the Bosnian Serbs with very substantial armaments. Or strictly speaking, they had left them in place when -- when they withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, but effectively it was simply a -- a transfer to their proxies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the withdrawal of support would have had what effect?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: It would have taken away their military advantage and it would have forced them to settle on -- on terms that might have made it impossible to bring about the -- the major relocation of populations that they had -- they had been pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally -- or perhaps almost a matter of opinion, but in light of Their Honours' questions: So far as the accused is concerned, the accused Milosevic, do you remember I asked you a question about attention between his doing one thing and doing another, and supporting the Bosnian Serbs, if it's found that he did, and holding their hand. What do you say this reveals as to his agenda or agendas, if they can be identified?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I'm -- I've never met the -- the accused, so I can really only comment as it was perceived in the Bosnian Serb leadership. They perceived him as an opportunist. They felt themselves to be true Serb nationalists, and they felt that Mr. Milosevic was trying to have it both ways; that he wanted to be conciliatory to the West and to rein in the Bosnian Serbs at the moment of their greatest victory, and yet he wanted to be supportive enough of the Serb national project, as they called it, to retain solid support of -- of those with genuinely nationalistic feelings. And it was this opportunism which they contrasted, for example, with Dr. Tudjman's pure nationalism, as they saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on. Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What view, if any, did the -- did your organisation take of this ambivalence -- apparent ambivalence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were very -- we were aware both of the basic level of support being provided by Serbia and we were aware of the -- the tensions between them. And as -- as you will recall, the international community at large, the Security Council and the contact group, were endeavouring to exacerbate it and to play on it. There were Security Council resolutions passed which offered relief of sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia if the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would put sanctions on and put pressure on and hold -- stay the hand of the Bosnian Serb party and the Croatian Serb party. So we were aware both of the basic level of support and we were aware and hoping to take some advantage from the differences that arose between them with respect to how far to push this Serbian national project in the face of very vigorous opposition from NATO, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is the position, are we to understand, as your organisation saw it or as you saw it, that on the one hand the Serb government and the accused were giving support to the Bosnian Serbs, materiel support, and general - correct me if I'm wrong in any of this, because I merely want to get it right - and general moral support to the Bosnian Serbs, but on the other hand the Serbs -- the accused was restraining the Bosnian Serbs where he thought it was in his interest to do so? I don't want to put words in your mouth, but -- but what was your impression? You were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was our impression. Our impression was that Milosevic was inclined as a gambler to leave the table with his winnings, that the Bosnian Serbs with the support of Serbia had done very well in the war. They had very quickly taken 70 per cent of the -- they were only 30 per cent of the population of Bosnia, but they had taken 70 per cent of the land area of Bosnia in a few weeks, at the beginning of the war. Milosevic's position -- in fact, I believe he publicly stated it, and including at the discussions on the Vance Owen Peace Plan -- was that they should now make substantial concessions in order to get a peace settlement and the relaxation of pressure from the West. That could be contrasted with the much more maximalist position of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would his position also be consistent with the -- the pressure that you say he was receiving from the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be consistent with that; though, I should state again that I've never met the accused. I got this only through my daily contacts with the Bosnian Serb leadership, so I see it through the lens of -- of their frustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we understand that. To make it clear, that of course we're going to have to make our minds up on these matters, on all the evidence in the case. But having the view or the impression of a witness who was actually there at the time is a matter for us to take into account. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this topic, can we look at tab 25, if we haven't looked at it already - perhaps we have - no. Is there a tab 25? No, there isn't. I'll move on from that and come back to what's marked as tab 25 as later, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I think we've covered really paragraphs 58 and 59 sufficiently. And I'll move on just to a couple of observations of paragraph 60, about General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've spoken already of the relationship, the developing relationship as you saw it, between the accused and Mladic. What was Mladic like in meetings? Just in a couple of sentences so we can have a picture of the man.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: He's -- he's a heavy set, large, red-faced --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not physically. I meant his behaviour. We know what he looks like.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: He was usually quiet for a very long time at the beginning of meetings. He would even stay in a separate room and play chess with General Gvero often. He would then take notes for the whole first session of a meeting. And then he would give answers that were not very -- he would give a presentation that was not very logical in its development. He would almost always mention the history of the Serbs, which he didn't really seem to know very well, and the suffering of his own family. His father had been killed during World War II. And he would very much emphasise the individual suffering of -- of Serbs. He was not a coherent and interlocutor really and he was given really to ending meetings with a series of -- of demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now go back to -- I think the Chamber will have a tab 25, even if --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 470, tab 25. It's a re--used document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. My error.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look at this document, please, if the witness has it?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No, I don't think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's coming to you. And it's your -- it's the report from Viktor Andreev of the 20th of September of 1994.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, on the first page, it speaks of the Serbs, entering into a lengthy discussion on the closing of the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia anxious about this, threatening various retaliatory measures and concerned about the possibility of that the Security Council will tighten sanctions on Pale. And Karadzic saying that such a move would put UNPROFOR in the position of having sided with the enemy. Saying, "If the international community treats us like a beast, then we will behave like a beast," and mentioning the use of utilities as a means of war. How does that fit in with the discussion we were having a question or so ago, including the topic of political influence, as opposed to just military?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Karadzic's view, as expressed to me and to others, was that they were vitally dependent on Serbia and that the threat by the Security Council, of which we as a United Nations organisation was seen to be an extension, was seen as an attack on the Bosnian Serbs' vital interests. He said that we were treating him as -- as a beast. I mean, it doesn't sound very sensible in English, but it might sound better in their language. He -- and he said that, you know, they would attack us and he would use utilities to -- the restriction of utilities such as gas and water to make life further miserable for the -- the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo unless the Security Council stopped threatening this essential lifeline between -- between him and his providers in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One more question on -- or a couple more questions on logistical and equipment support, paragraph 63. I think you've covered everything, pay and equipment, but you haven't dealt with air cover. Was there ever any evidence available to you of Serbian air cover being provided?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, there was a no-fly zone of course above Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so aircraft of all three sides did violate it. But when they did, they were at risk of being shot down, so there was not much air military activity. Four Galeb, I believe, light fighter strike aircraft were launched from Banja Luka and shot down in 1994. Another one was shot down later -- oh, sorry, crashed in Cazin later in 1994. When they crashed on Bosnian Muslim territory, when we were able to investigate them, as certainly we did, and took photographs in the case of the one that crashed in Cazin, the pilots were wearing Yugoslav uniforms, and indeed the Yugoslav press reported their funerals in -- in Yugoslavia. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 20, please, in the Exhibit 546. It deals with another weapon system in a report of the 1st of December, 1994. And this report, in paragraph 2, speaks of General Rose at a meeting explaining that the Serb decision to activate their air defence system had heightened tensions significantly, and pointing out that NATO aircraft responded automatically when locked onto or when fired upon. What was the weapons system referred to here or touched upon here?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I believe this is referring to the activation of the SAM-2 missile system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: The SAM- 2 missile system, of course, is a radar-based system rather than a heat-based one, so you can detect the radars when they lock on. And the first time this happened was in late 1994. Now, the SAM-2 system is physically large and it is complex and the fact that it didn't -- it wasn't active in Republika Srpska, Serb-held territory in Bosnia, prior to this date and then it was able to be activated when the level of NATO air coverage became more aggressive was seen as almost certainly being facilitated by -- by Serbia, because the only other places they could have got them were from the Muslims or the Croats, which didn't seem possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 21, please. I haven't marked a passage on this, so I'll deal with it in the ordinary way. Was there a meeting of the Bosnian Serb leadership in Sanski Most in March 1995 where Mladic spoke of RS strategy?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb leadership told us that there was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was their change in strategy?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: There was an understanding that they would have to become -- they would have to move on the -- onto the offensive in 1995 and to move away from the defensive posture of 1993 and 1994 in able to -- in order to end the war before the Republic of Croatia could become a threat or before the Bosnian Muslims were able to turn their numerical advantage into a -- into success on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're coming up to Srebrenica. Just before we do, look at how you prepared a report on that, one or two other things. What do you know -- what did you discover about the presence of Mladic in or around Belgrade at the time of and leading up to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: The -- the massacres at Srebrenica I believe took place on or after the 14th of July. The town fell on Tuesday, the 11th of July. And at least one member of the contact group said that he had seen Mr. Milosevic in Serbia with General Mladic on the -- the 7th of July, and that is one day after the -- the attack had -- had begun but still well before the -- the fall of the town and the massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at tab 22, if you can help us with this. Do you recognise this document, first of all, or not?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes; I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you summarise for us the effect of this, because we are pressed for time. It comes under paragraph 68 on the summary.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. After the fall of Srebrenica, the Serbs almost immediately attacked Zepa. And while Zepa was falling and there was great confusion, the Bosnian Serbs approached us very urgently and said that they wanted to arrange a so-called all-for-all prisoner exchange. In theory, this would have been very attractive to the Muslims because many more -- prior to Srebrenica, many more Muslims were being held by the Serbs than Serbs were being held by Muslims. Of course, at the time of this meeting, the killings had already taken place at Srebrenica and -- but we didn't know that, nor did the Bosnian Muslims know that. And the Serbs were trying to say it should be all for all, not counting Srebrenica, which we'll put into a different -- a different batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your inference from their enthusiasm was what?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, they were very nervous, because they thought that knowledge of the killings at Srebrenica would come out and then they would have no chance of getting back the -- the Serb prisoners held by the -- held by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who on the Bosnian Serb side was conducting these negotiations? Because if your calculation is correct, then there would be knowledge in whoever was conducting those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: General Mladic sent messages. He did not appear in person. He was actually in Zepa at this time with General Tolimir and General Panic, the Muslim commander. And he sent two people, Lieutenant Colonel Indjic and an officer he always -- he -- a person he always sent for prisoner exchanges called Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you at any time receive from the Bosnian Serbs any explanation for the people missing, killed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No. However, I think that the first survivor of the massacres came out on the 19th or the 20th and spoke on Tuzla television. And after that, there were a series of investigations leading up to Mrs. Albright's presentation in the Security Council of aerial photographs of disturbed earth where previously people had been seen gathering. And during that period, as the story was coming out, the Serbs broke off these -- these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on just to get the chronology right and then we'll come back to your Srebrenica report and one or two other matters. On the 30th of August, did you send the text of a letter from Mr. Akashi to Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: The 30th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you don't recall it, it doesn't necessarily matter, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And on the 11th of October, did you receive letters from Muratovic and Buha agreeing to a cease-fire effective for the 12th of October? We can see that on tab 23.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. That is the instrument which ends the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a short document. We don't need to look at it in any great detail. Before I conclude these questions, just this: Was there any -- within the United Nations and elsewhere, was there a debate and -- as to what the safe areas were aimed at and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. There was a very --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 75. Summarise it, please.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: There was an active debate as to whether or not the safe area concept was there to protect people or to protect areas, which would later become part of Bosnian Muslim territory. There was great concern about the concept within UNPROFOR because it was felt that the Security Council mandate, which was to deter attacks on them, was not militarily possible with the forces provided, and that the populations were therefore significantly at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we now could come to the second exhibit. Before I produce it, because I'm anxious not to burden you with paper that you won't want to have, can I explain what it is and what it may become. First of all, the -- the first, whatever it is, 20 - 37, 36 -- 35 tabs in this document are UN Council resolutions. Now, they are really public documents that in the vernacular of the Tribunal could self-propel themselves into exhibit status. Nevertheless, it occurred to me it might be quite helpful for there to be an exhibit that had the relevant ones collected and numbered and they could be added to, and this witness could, as it were, nominally produce them. Although, I don't want to take any time going through them with him, and he doesn't hold himself out as a particular expert on them, although he could make just a few observations about them. The last document in this possible exhibit is his report on Srebrenica, about which I can get him to tell you. It's, of course, a long document, and I'm not asking that we go through all of it. And I'm certainly not asking that a great deal of time should be taken on it, unless it's appropriate to do so. But it seems to me that that possibly is a document that the Chamber would like to have available. And if so, what I would propose to do -- what I would do is to get him to explain his methodology and probably beyond identifying paragraphs that the Chamber might find interesting to read, perhaps, if it has the time in the next break, not to take him through it in detail. But I'm very much in the Chamber's hands, first, as to whether these self-propelling documents should more conveniently be produced by this witness; and second, whether he, having given his evidence, it would nevertheless be helpful to hear how he prepared this report on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The tab number 37 in that binder is a report of the Security Council mission. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- I think 37 may be a mistitle. 36 is the Srebrenica report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other document, I haven't yet -- the report on the Security Council mission pursuant to Resolution 819 of the 30th of April, I'm not sure that we have that. If we do -- no, that's been incorrectly attached to the Srebrenica report. It's the last few pages of it. You'll see it's a different -- a slightly different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're asking 37 to come out, so we can understand it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, we're including it really as part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit this exhibit and get the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 547, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to -- as to the Security Council resolutions, there are a couple more that the witness believes may be helpful. We were discussing it just before he came to give evidence this morning. They've been made available. Over the break I'll find a way of agreeing with the legal officers how they should be included so that this exhibit can be available for the addition of any other resolutions that others may find useful or appropriate to add later in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harland, so far as the resolutions are concerned -- and you may not be able to remember the numbers. Just give a sketch, if you will, of what you think is the material and important histories and then we can track them down later if necessary.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: There are a very large number of Security Council resolutions with respect to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. The first significant one, I think, is -- is 713 of 1991, which imposes an arms embargo on all parties to the -- the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's an additional one that we're going to have to add to the bundle. Yes.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: And there are a very large number dealing with issues such as the provision of humanitarian aid and the authorisation of the United Nations to use force to ensure its delivery, such as Resolution 770 and 776. Those were both 1992, I think. There were also a series of resolutions setting up and mandating the United Nations and NATO in the deterrence of attacks on six designated safe areas, so-called safe areas, including Srebrenica. Those would be resolutions 819, 824, and 836 I think of 1993. Then there are additional resolutions seeking to induce the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to become more cooperative by either lifting sanctions on them in return for them establishing some blockade on the -- the Drina and -- and a very large number of -- of other measures taken by the international community in the context of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab 36 of this second exhibit of yours, 547, which is your report to the Secretary-General. And we're going to take this very briefly. Explain first who instructed you, where you prepared it, how you prepared it. And the Chamber may want to turn to what is on the bottom right-hand corner, page number 111, I think, which identifies your -- your various interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yeah. First, I should say it's not my report. It's -- to the Secretary-General. It's the Secretary-General's report to the General Assembly of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I just drafted it. The -- and researched it. The -- and I should also say that the list of people on page 111 is -- interview -- is very much not complete because a substantial number of people who were interviewed asked not to be identified. For the -- the methodology, the methodology was the -- to go over the reports of the United Nations personnel in Srebrenica and dealing with Srebrenica. And I was given unrestricted access to the -- to the classified files of the United Nations for that. And also to conduct interviews with the -- the major participants. Unfortunately, particularly as -- with respect to this trial, I didn't interview anybody in Serbia. I did send faxes to people, but unfortunately NATO was attacking Serbia at the time. It was written during the spring and summer of 1999, including General Perisic and others, and they agreed to meet me in fact. But -- but they were not able to -- to meet with me because of that, that war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to any conclusions in the report as against the accused in this case, anything adverse, anything positive, or simply neutral?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Well, as -- sorry. As we said before, there is one -- there is no direct connection established in the report between Mr. Milosevic and the massacres that took place at Srebrenica. Of course, prior to it, the Serb army was getting a lot of support, and prior to the fall he obviously met with Mladic, so he knew there was an attack going on, but somehow the -- the -- the problem as regards both our outrage and the law is not so much the -- the attacks, of which there were many, but the massacres, and this report makes no link to Mr. Milosevic with those massacres. And in fact there is one piece of evidence, as I mentioned to you before, which somewhat inclines me to believe that Mr. Milosevic was not involved in commissioning the massacres, which is that immediately after the fall of Srebrenica, the two days after the Serbs began their attack on Zepa, and Mr. Milosevic did in fact help to save some of the men of Zepa. At least according to interviews -- I did not interview Mr. Milosevic, but at least according to the interviews I conducted with Mr. Muratovic, who's a Bosnian government official, and with Carl Bildt, who was then an international peace negotiator, when Zepa was falling, they wanted to ensure that the men wouldn't be massacred, even though they didn't yet know about the Srebrenica massacres. And because Zepa is very close to the Serbian border, some of them were fleeing by rafts in -- into Serbia. And according to Dr. Muratovic, he did call Mr. Bildt and asked Mr. Bildt to speak to Mr. Milosevic to ensure that those who fled into Serbia would not be killed or mistreated. And according to both Bildt and to Muratovic, Milosevic did that and the people were detained, which is normal and customary, I believe, under the rules of war, and then were released after the war. And as far as I am -- or at least as far as those two interviewees were concerned, Mr. Milosevic played a helpful role.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I would very respectfully propose is that the Chamber looks at the summary, starting at paragraph 79. It can see and could read more swiftly than I could a summary of what may be some interesting paragraphs, going on to paragraph 92 of the summary. It deals with paragraph 501 of the report. So either the summary or indeed the original paragraphs of the report might conveniently be read, if the Chamber thought this appropriate, in the break. And I have then only one other question of this witness to cover, which I've overlooked, before I shall conclude, and it relates, in fact, to the earlier exhibit, 546, and to tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could just briefly look at it. I don't think it's necessary to display this on the overhead projector. This is a document not of your own authorship, I think, but it deals with something that Mladic said about the eastern enclaves. Was what he said reported to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. I should say -- yeah, all other meetings referred to, I think, in this exhibit I was at. This meeting I was not at, but it took place in Vlasenica, the command post of the Drina Corps. General Smith, with his military assistant, James Baxter, met with General Mladic and General Mladic did seem to indicate - and James Baxter reported back to me orally - that the Serbs had indicated that they wished to attack the eastern enclaves during 1995 in order to reduce them just to purely guarded camps, in order to free up troops for other essential military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That concludes the evidence, does it, apart from some tidying up?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from some tidying up, if I think of it, after the break, and apart from possibly reading the summary in the way that I've suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think it would be difficult to cut short dramatically the accused's cross-examination on this witness, in the light of the evidence he's given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I accept that. I made great progress in the first session, but it became perhaps impossible to move as fast in the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're being handed two additional resolutions, we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. These are the two other resolutions. If the Chamber thinks it's a good idea to have a library, then the obviously sensible thing would be for them to be fitted in in a chronological way rather than to simply tag them on at the end. That could probably be done by fitting them in at the appropriate place chronologically and amending the index for two entries that contain two resolutions. We can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with that after the adjournment. I don't know that we do think it's a good idea to have a library, but we'll add these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whenever you mention a library, Mr. Nice, I'm a little intimidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to intimidate. I simply know that for some materials -- some examples of materials, it probably should be available. That was my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one -- one matter that I ought to have tidied up, and I'll do so now, if I may. The Chamber may want to have paragraph 77 of the summary in mind and also to look at Exhibit 547, tab 37, the tab that I'd mislaid but which is the report of the Security Council mission of April 1993, where Diego Arria from Venezuela was the coordinator. And if the Chamber would be good enough to go to page number 5 of that tab, the page numbers being at the top. You'll see that at the foot of that page, the report reads as follows: "The council should note that when it was discussing Resolution 819, it did not know that negotiations involving the force commander of UNPROFOR had been taking place and that UNPROFOR had participated actively in the drafting and in the process of convincing the Bosnian commander to sign the agreement. The alternative could have been a massacre of 25.000 people." Now, this is a report, Mr. Harland, if not compiled by, participated in by Diego Arria in April 1993. I think reference to it is made in your report and the distribution of that earlier United Nations or Security Council report could have alerted people to the views of some that massacre at Srebrenica was a possibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, as you've made clear to us and in paragraph 77 of the summary, page 24, would not yourself have anticipated a massacre?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No, certainly not on that scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not on that scale.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've explained to the Judges what the pattern of takeovers, including killings were in other places.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by reference to Diego Arria's report, you may recognise that others held other views.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to get the last two tabs, which we were referring to earlier in 547. Yes, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Resolution 713 will be tab 38 and Resolution 776 will be tab 39 of 547.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, I see that you arrived in Sarajevo in June 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right after you got your doctoral degree at the Fletcher School of law and diplomacy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, right after it was awarded. Actually, I'd stopped studying several years earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you then live in America? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No. Prior to -- while I studied at the Fletcher School and at Harvard universities, which is until 1991, I lived in the United States. Between 1991 and 1993, I lived in the -- the Great Lakes region of Africa, with the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you start working for the United Nations? Just after you graduated, after 1991?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. I had some brief earlier service before I went back and finished my Ph.D., but effectively in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have a scholarship at the time?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the answer -- the question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who gave the scholarship, I think. The Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy has a fund for their own -- for scholars they accept and Harvard University did -- and both organisations funded me almost fully to complete my degrees at their two universities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 3 of your statement, you say, they sent me to Sarajevo -- "I was posted to Sarajevo, rather, Bosnia-Herzegovina in June 1993 as a Civil Affairs Officer, under Viktor Andreev at Bosnia-Herzegovina Command based in Kiseljak"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was it that posted you in Sarajevo actually?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR. I arrived in Zagreb and their office of civil affairs determined that I should work in -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: By then you were already an employee of the United Nations for already two years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that there were two aspects of your work; political reporting and political work. Is that right? That's what you say in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you care to elaborate on that? What did political reporting involve and what did political work involve?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Sure. The political reporting was to make -- to communicate what had happened at meetings participated in by UN senior staff in Sarajevo with the Bosnian government or Bosnian Serb leadership, and that involved a regular weekly report and it also involved a -- a daily reporting on whatever meetings we had been to during the day. The political work was to participate in those meetings. And we were normally either trying to negotiate the evacuation of civilians or the restoration of electricity to hospitals, and a range of -- and sometimes even prisoner exchanges or -- or dead bodies or -- a range of things that needed to be negotiated between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serbs in which they asked for the United Nations to serve as some sort of intermediary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is roughly what the subject of your work was. I noticed during your testimony here that the greatest part of your testimony was dedicated to military matters, but you did not deal in military matters, to the best of my understanding.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I mean because when -- when you're -- when we negotiated a -- a cease-fire or an anti-sniping agreement or the withdrawal of Serb forces from Mount Igman, we would always -- I mean, I would always be present and would participate. So the military matters were very much at the centre of -- of UNPROFOR's concerns. They were almost as important as the -- as the humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But just now you used an expression, if I can put it that way. You said, "the Serb national project." You used it several times. You understand this project to mean ethnic cleansing, to the best of my understanding. How did you get that idea, that there is something called the Serb national project, and how could that mean ethnic cleansing of any kind?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That was actually a phrase used by our -- our Serb partners in Pale, Professor Koljevic and -- and Dr. Zametica. They would -- they would often describe their war effort as -- and what they were trying to produce as a part of the -- the Serbian national project. And in that -- that element of it, the element of it with which they and we were involved, was their attempt to create a -- an overwhelmingly Serb territory that would be either independent or highly autonomous and the population of which would be overwhelmingly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when you started testifying today, I think that you first spoke about a meeting where Radovan Karadzic said that their priority was to have Izetbegovic or, as you put it, the Muslim government should come to the negotiating table, to negotiate the peace agreement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, as far as I could see from the documents that you presented here, he said that in their approach, they did not deny the right of people to remain in their own homes, wherever they lived, irrespective of ethnicity, or the right of those who left due to war operations to come back, no matter what kind of delineations may be made.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how do you link that up to a project of ethnic cleansing? If this kind of clear-cut position was presented, and you spoke about it too, and you also presented at the very outset a paper to that effect.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That's what they claimed. But what they actually did was to prosecute a -- a campaign of -- of ethnic cleansing. And I should say when -- when we asked Dr. Karadzic about what was actually happening on the ground, he would say that "Well, some old people will probably want to remain," Serbs in the Muslim areas or Muslims in the Serb areas, but he was clearly envisaging the overwhelming bulk of the population remaining in Serb territory to be Serb and in Muslim-held territory to be -- to be Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is what was being envisaged. However, as far as the right of people is concerned, to remain in any one of these territories, he did not challenge that right in any way; isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, you say that Serbia extended support, which of course is not in dispute, both to Serbs in the Republika Srpska and in the Serbian Krajina Republic, but you linked that up with this ethnic cleansing project, which is proved false by what we have just referred to. So how could you come to the conclusion that Serbia - and I personally - supported ethnic cleansing and that the whole project was a project of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Because what was actually happening and the way in which the Bosnian Serbs were actually using the support provided by Serbia was certainly ethnic cleansing. And in fact, they would -- they would even boast about it. I -- at -- at lunch I recall Dr.-- or sorry, General Mladic talking about how they had taken Visegrad, how they had taken Rogatica, how they had taken Brcko, how they had taken some other people. And -- and at one meeting when he was actually challenged and said, "Well, didn't you have hundreds of tanks provided by the Yugoslav armies for this -- this purpose?" he -- he readily acknowledged that. So there is certainly a gap which was barely -- barely disguised between what they claimed was the legal rights of the non-Serb population in the area that they would establish as Republika Srpska and -- and the reality, which was when they entered a town, the -- the non-Serb population was either killed or removed or terrorised until they fled, with a few small exceptions. You know, there were still Muslim villages around Bijeljina when I -- when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I hope, Mr. Harland, as you spent a lot of time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as Mr. Nice pointed out, you were the longest-serving UN officer over there, you know very well - and I'm sure you visited Serbia as well - so you are familiar with the political situation in Serbia and you must know that ethnic cleansing in the political vernacular of Serbia was defined as a crime. It could not have, under any circumstances, been part of the political approach to the settlement of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: It was certainly a part of the -- the military events unfolding on the ground when I was there, and it continued to be that until the -- the end of the war. I mean, I -- I agree with you that there may have been legal provisions against ethnic cleansing and even rhetorical statements to that effect, but in fact the -- the -- the stated purpose of what was going on on their side was the creation of a largely Serb populated territory which they would call Republika Srpska. And they were quite -- quite open about that. And I must say that at some of the meetings some of the participants, such as Professor Plavsic, even said that -- directly said, "It's good if all the non-Serbs go. We want them to go. We're not living well together. Let them -- let them all leave when we take over certain areas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, your reference to rhetorical statements against ethnic cleansing, could you give us an illustration of some of those and in what context they were made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Milosevic has just touched on -- on one. And in fact, it's one of -- one of the -- the few I remember Dr. Karadzic making. He -- he would expand on the same idea sometimes and even say that he had a mechanism in mind for setting up an internationally funded sort of housing exchange so that somebody, you know, of nationality X in a zone controlled by nationality Y could exchange a house with somebody in the opposite situation. So at least at the level of that type of discussion Mr. Milosevic is right. There is -- it was not an insistence that they be removed by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as forcible removal of people and ethnic cleansing are concerned, as you stayed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I assume you cannot attribute this only to one side but there were such instances on all three sides, instances that could be defined as "ethnic cleansing" and as a criminal act. I don't think there's a single side that could be said to have been completely innocent in that respect.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the position of Serbia now. You came in 1993, as I see from your statement, practically one month after the Assembly at which the Vance Owen Plan was reviewed at Pale, the Assembly of Republika Srpska. And I assume you're well informed about it. And do you remember what I defined as goals when advocating the acceptance of the Vance Owen Plan? Let me remind you, that the goals are for the Serb people to be free and equal, not more, not less than that. Is that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, our support -- and I spoke at that very Assembly meeting and said that "With this plan, the Serb people have restored their right to be treated equally as a constituent nation and with this plan its fate will be in its hands, as it will be in the hands of the other two peoples on an equal footing and in freedom." Isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That's correct. Though, there was an enormous gap between what was said and the actual situation on the ground, what they were doing with the Serbian support, which was really --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is a question as to what each side was doing and with what support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must let the witness finish what he was saying. Now, Mr. Harland, is there anything you want to add? You were cut off in the middle of a sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was just saying that that's -- that's true of what Mr. Milosevic says of his own presentation. And one of the most frustrating things about the conflict was the enormous gap between the relatively high-minded comments that could be made at forums such as that one and the -- the reality on the ground. For example, by the time he -- he made that comment, there were already well over a million people in Bosnia and Herzegovina who had been forced to flee their homes, and many of those people, with whom I would often meet, had been forced to flee their homes because of assets, support provided by -- by Serbia to the -- to the Bosnian Serb party. And they -- the Bosnian Serbs were grateful for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us make things quite clear regarding this point. It's not quite clear to me, because throughout Serbia in 1991 with the Vance Plan, which was implemented, as is stated in the report of the Secretary-General, and later on, with respect to the Vance-Owen Plan and the five other plans that we supported, I don't understand how you can view our policies - I mean the policies of Serbia and my own personal policy - as opportunism rather than a consistent and uninterrupted effort to achieve a peaceful settlement in the former Yugoslavia. Could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No, I didn't consider it an uninterrupted effort to bring about a peaceful solution to the conflict in Yugoslavia, at least not as far as I saw it. The -- what I saw was large amounts of Serbian support, military support principally, enabling the Bosnian Serb party to control 70 per cent of Bosnia and Herzegovina and then to make demands for a final peace settlement that were obviously unjust. So for example, the Serbs would come to us and say, "We will -- we will not accept any of the international plans on the -- on the table, including the one which you referred to about the meeting in Pale, which you will recall that the Bosnian Serb party, who, much supported by Serbian military assets, were successfully able to -- to reject the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But those plans, which we supported and some of which were also supported by the leadership at Pale, they never implied that 70 per cent of the territory should remain in the hands of the Serbs. Isn't that right, Mr. Harland? You remember the plan of the contact group, for instance, which was supported by the leadership in Pale. Or to move even further back, you remember the Cutileiro Plan, before the outbreak of the war, which in fact all three parties signed. So not one of those plans --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know you mustn't pile up questions like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree to all -- all the questions. Yeah. That's true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is an intellectual and he can understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But he can't answer a series of questions. One at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you insist on economy, and I am using my time by asking certain summary questions. But I hope that the witness is not bothered by them and he's fully able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When talking about Karadzic's insistence on the Muslim side to come to the negotiating table when peace plans were discussed, it was always a peace plan that was proposed by international mediators. Afterwards, there was the Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, several plans of the contact group, which again the Serbs accepted and the leadership at Pale. So it wasn't any imposition of a Serbian plan but rather that negotiations be held on the proposal on the table made by international mediators. In your period of time, the plan was drafted by Owen and Stoltenberg; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That is correct, but we objected very strongly to the use of shelling and sniping and the cutting off of food as an instrument by which the Serbs could convince the Bosnian Muslims to accept an -- an agreement which was -- was unattractive to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you, in the examination-in-chief, also mention that talking to Karadzic you heard and you were able to see for yourself as well that it was the Serb side that was having enormous problems caused by the Muslim side as a result of sniping and shooting at their lines? Wasn't that so? That was the reason for them to respond to these provocations. Didn't you mention something along those lines a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I don't believe I -- I did mention that. And certainly, at least in the area which I was serving in, at least 90 per cent of the -- the casualties by sniping and shelling took place on the -- the Muslim side of the line. That sometimes included Serbs and Croats who lived on the Muslim side of the line. But the overwhelming bulk of the -- of the civilian casualties were on the -- the Muslim side of the line, and what was particularly alarming to us was that Dr. Karadzic and his associates would directly say, "We will use this Serbian-supported war machine to make life impossible for the civilians," to terrorise the civilians in order to reach a particular political goal. We -- we found that very, very cynical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I hear for the first time that anyone from the leadership of Republika Srpska could have told you that their aim was to terrorise civilians, and you're claiming that that is what they told you, to terrorise civilians was their goal?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact, I believe that in the morning we already had an -- an exhibit in which we quoted Dr. Karadzic as saying that if certain political -- if certain political conditions weren't met, in terms of the Muslims going to negotiate with him in Geneva, that he would cut off the water and the electricity to the civilian population of Sarajevo. When the Security Council said that it would attempt to make a blockade between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska, he said that he would -- the Bosnian Serbs, using their Serb-provided military, would behave as beasts. And he made direct threats of shelling, anyway, both against us and against Sarajevo. So in fact, it was, unfortunately, quite explicit that they would use their military apparatus to -- to terrorise the population in the hope of -- of getting the political outcome they -- they wanted, which of course was a recognition in -- in law and in international practice of the -- the territory they had -- they had captured in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he said that the proposal tabled by international mediators should be discussed at a negotiating table; isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I think the one I was quoting was this document of the 20th of September, 1994, which is actually not about peace negotiations at all. It's -- it's about the efforts by the Security Council to bring about a closure of the border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnian Serb-held territory, where he claimed that he would treat us like a beast, he would do other things. He said at the same meeting he was going to flatten parts of Sarajevo. He was -- Dr.-- Mr. Krajisnik made similar threats, thinly veiled threats. He said, "It would be difficult to stop Serb soldiers from shooting at UN airplanes bringing humanitarian assistance"; in other words, given what we knew about their relatively strong chain of command and control, they were directly threatening both us and the Bosnian Muslims to achieve a particular aim. And in particular they were saying that their main instrument would be the cutting off of humanitarian supplies and water and electricity and gas using the military assets they had from -- from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They said that they would use the military assets that they had from Serbia? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: They didn't -- they did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Harland. Do you know how the army of Republika Srpska was formed? All armies in the territory of the former Yugoslavia were created out of former members of the JNA and others that joined them.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. They had a continuing and ongoing relationship with Serbia, which they relied on for support, and which they acknowledged openly up to the level of General Mladic. And indeed, when the link between Republika Srpska and its armed forces and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was threatened by the Security Council, they became particularly aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was not called in question by the Security Council but by our side, because at that time we were bringing pressure to bear for the peace plan to be accepted. It was not the pressure of the Security Council but our endeavours to have the peace plan adopted. That is common knowledge. You can find that in all the newspapers from those times, just as you can find, I assume, also that the government of Serbia or, rather, the leadership of Serbia was most emphatically opposed to the shelling of Sarajevo. I assume you know that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two questions there. Mr. Harland, if you'd like to answer them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second one: The government of Serbia may have been opposed at some level to the shelling of Sarajevo, which would be appropriate, because that was not a shelling that we felt had any military value. It was a dispersed fire that only had a -- a sort of terroristic effect. And if the government of Serbia was opposed to that, it -- it certainly wasn't evident on the ground. On the contrary, the Serb commanders said they had links to Belgrade, and at critical moments when we sought intervention from you or from Belgrade that was able to -- such as during the Gorazde crisis -- that was able to affect the -- the behaviour of the Bosnian Serb army. In other words, there clearly was a link between Belgrade and the Bosnian Serb army, and yet the Bosnian Serb army continued, day after day after day for a thousand days, to fire a minimum of several hundred shells a day into the civilian centre of Sarajevo. So when the government of Serbia said that it was opposed to the shelling of Sarajevo, I believe that they were being dishonest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That may be your opinion, but as you're talking about the influence of the political leadership of Serbia and my own influence, and giving examples of that, do you have a single example showing that that influence was used to instigate the conflict or, rather, do all the examples indicate that all the influence and pressure was brought to bear to stop, to halt the conflict?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: We were able to detect direct intervention by yourself or by others in Belgrade on the armed forces of Republika Srpska only at a few key points in time; most evidently around Gorazde but also during the Igman and -- and Bjelasnica case. Those certainly gave us the -- the impression that the Bosnian Serbs military, regardless of whether they were playing a positive role or were playing a negative role, were very amenable to influence by you; thus -- or by others in Belgrade. And thus, the fact that nothing was done to restrain the Bosnian Serb army around Sarajevo, and in other places - you know, including Srebrenica - we -- we took as meaning that you either acquiesced or supported these activities, because we could see demonstrated in the pattern of behaviour a capacity to influence these -- these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, international mediators who came to see me - and you mentioned Churkin and Akashi and others - wanted to help, to stop the war. Serbia -- and I personally for my part did my best to wield all my influence in order to stop the war and to support the peace plans or, rather, to stop having individual situations of the kind that you're describing; that is to say, situations of crisis, to overcome them in order to enable us to solve issues peacefully. So that is the experience gained from each of the examples that you have quoted. Is that something you're aware of or not?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: What I'm aware of is that the -- that you clearly had a capacity to influence the behaviour of the Bosnian Serb armed forces. We saw it. We could ask them about it. There was a large amount of financial and materiel support they got, and yet nothing was done to -- to stop the shelling of Sarajevo or the sniping or the attacks on the safe areas or -- or even the massacres that followed the fall of -- of Srebrenica.
