I've already made something of an exception for Zepa, but I think that the -- the pattern of acquiescence in the crimes committed against the civilian population of Bosnia and Herzegovina is -- is relatively -- is relatively clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot ascribe that to Serbia in any way. Do you know that up until the events in Srebrenica and the attack on the safe zone, I heard about that from Carl Bildt and that was the first time I had heard of it. So what does Serbia have to do with various military operations of the army of Republika Srpska, and especially with the one in Srebrenica? And nobody knew about that in Serbia, and even I heard about it for the first time from Carl Bildt, for example. And it is true that Carl Bildt, whether on that particular day or the following day, asked permission -- or rather, there was a message that some Muslim brigades should be saved and allowed to cross the Drina. And we accepted that. There were 840-odd people. We didn't arrest them, as you said, take them prisoner, but we put them in the camp on Mount Tara, and I insisted that the diplomats from all countries in Belgrade should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are cross-examining now, not making a speech. What do you want the witness to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I was saying was this: Are you claiming that there was a chain of command from the army of Republika Srpska down to Yugoslavia and that we were in fact in command of the army of Republika Srpska? Is that what you're saying -- and its operations?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: There was support, maintenance, influence from Belgrade, and Belgrade used that support, maintenance, influence to -- to direct a number of outcomes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it apparently did nothing to prevent over a period of some years the -- the shelling of Sarajevo, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean we could have done more than we did?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Oh, vastly more. The Bosnian Serbs were almost entirely dependent on support from Serbia and had a - as they themselves recognised - and had a serious effort been made to restrain them, I think that they would certainly have been responsive. They told us as much themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the efforts undertaken by Serbia to find a peaceful solution were not serious ones, or do you consider that what we should have done was to withhold any assistance to them and allow them to be killed, just like many others were killed and fell casualty?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I think that the cause of peace was not advanced by giving them the full military support they needed to secure, ethnically cleanse, and hold very large territories. I think that it is true that -- probably true that Serbia was -- wanted a peace agreement and wanted the Bosnian Serbs to give up more than they were willing to give up and that that may have caused differences between Belgrade and Pale. But I do not believe that that led to significant withdrawal of support by Belgrade for Pale, despite the fact that it could have done that and despite the fact it could have influenced events such as the daily killing year after year of civilians in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we did wield all our influence and do everything we could to stop the war. Now you say that that was not so, that it was otherwise. But never mind. There are others, and we can clear that point up. Tell me, Mr. Harland, in paragraph 5 you say that it was your task to make political assessments, prepare political assessments. Did you do that on a retrospective basis, or did you assess what might happen in the future and what had happened in the past?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: There was a limited amount of -- a limited attempt to identify the course of events in the coming weeks and month. The principal object was simply to relay information and to try to understand that information from Pale and from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, as sources of information, those that you used, you mention the warring sides themselves to start off with and then briefings of commanders, international organisations, and general UNPROFOR information; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That would be the gist of it, of your basis and groundwork. Now, assessing the participation of the warring sides in putting forward and placing their information, how much came from the Serb side and how much from the Muslim side would you say?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I would say we met about the same with the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale and Lukavica and with the Bosnian Muslim leadership in -- in Sarajevo. We also, of course, had, I mean, some independence or information on -- we had the United Nations military observers who were taking note of who was firing at who and at what rate and were checking with mortuaries and Ministers of Health and so on. But between the parties in Sarajevo, I think we probably saw both sides about -- about the same, and we often saw them together in the context of various negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean as far as the warring sides were concerned, they were sort of balanced, and all the others came from international organisations, did they not, all this other information? Were there various non-governmental organisations as sources of information too? I assume so.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we had -- we had some contact with the local population, both on the Serb side and on the Bosnian government side. So, for example, we used to monitor the price of various commodities to check their availability; we used to monitor through UNHCR the humanitarian situation; ICRC would provide information on missing persons. So yes, we had a -- a range of sources. But I think that the -- the principal sources were the Bosnian government leadership, the Bosnian Serb leadership, and information directly generated by UNPROFOR or UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, to speed up a little bit, before I move on to the chronology of events, as you present them in your statement, let me ask you this first: Do you know how many Serbs were killed in Sarajevo during the war there, during that period of time, 1991-1992?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: No, I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the figure being at 10.000 from anybody, that kind of figure? Because you said you had frequent meetings with people close to the leadership of Republika Srpska, for example, or even with the top representatives themselves. But you never heard anything about that, did you?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That would not be a credible figure. That would not be a serious figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know that we still don't know about the fate of some 5.000 Serbs from Sarajevo and its environs?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: That is not correct, according to the number of tracing requests that have been lodged with the International Committee of the Red Cross, nor is it in any way consistent with the -- the number of people who have either appeared at the mortuary or who were killed, for example, by the supporters of Caco and buried without being taken to the mortuary. There certainly were Serb victims, some of them killed by -- by Muslims, like Caco, some of them killed or wounded by the -- the Serb guns and snipers around the city. But if I had to make an educated guess, I would put the number in the low hundreds. It's still a lot. It's terrible. But it's certainly nothing like 10.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the figure I have here. But tell me this, please: The figure I mentioned and the Serbs missing to the present day from Sarajevo and around it, do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: When I was in -- serving in Sarajevo, the -- the numbers of tracing requests lodged with the International Committee of the Red Cross - and this number normally corresponds with missing people - was certainly not in the order of many thousands. It was much -- much, much lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in view of the fact that there are facts and figures about that, I need not discuss the matter with you. Mr. Harland, as you gave us a detailed explanation as to what you consider to be the goals of -- the goals prescribed by Republika Srpska, from what you were able to assess from your talks with Koljevic, Plavsic, and others, and all the other people you talked to - I don't know who they all were - but what were the goals of the other warring side, that is to say, the BH army? Because I assume that you probably had a clear-cut idea of those goals too.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I think they were much more divided in what they wanted than the Bosnian Serb party. I think that there was one group which felt that the Muslims are the largest community in Bosnia and Herzegovina and therefore they had an interest in keeping Bosnia and Herzegovina together as a single state in which they would not be threatened in any way because they would be almost a majority. And, in fact, of course there is -- there is language in Mr. Izetbegovic's Islamic declaration which refers to the -- the role that will be played by a Muslim community once they become a majority in a -- in a given country. I believe that there was also a -- a tendency among Bosnian -- some Bosnian Muslims to try and create their own compact territory, that is, to pursue goals similar to those of the Serbs and Croats; in other words, to -- to seek to establish a -- a territory on which they would be the -- if not the exclusive community, the overwhelmingly dominant community. And in fact, these two tendencies even debated each other publicly sometimes, such as at the National Assembly meeting that took place in Sarajevo on -- at the Holiday Inn in September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- all right. Yes, I understand that. But since you read the Islamic declaration of Alija Izetbegovic, I assume that you know about his attitude and position that there cannot be any cohabitation between Islam and non-Islamic institutions. I'm paraphrasing it of course now. But I assume you know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the views he put down in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you then consider that the Serbs could have accepted a state conceived along those lines, Serbs -- the Serbs which had -- who had until then lived as a nation on a footing of equality with everybody else in the area? Could they have accepted that?

utterances.speaker: David Harland
utterances.text: I think that as in our earlier discussion about what people say rhetorically and what they actually do, it's important to discuss reality. Now, I -- when you mention the figure of 10.000 Serbs possibly killed in Sarajevo, I would mention that I lived in Sarajevo for -- for many years, and it was not an atmosphere of terror. I immediately accept that there was a -- there were crimes committed, but in general -- and there was some level of discrimination against non-Muslims in some areas. But I would say that in general the political structures established by the Bosnian Muslims - and at the beginning of the war this was under the leadership of Izetbegovic - were less violently intolerant than the structures established by either the Serb or Croat party. That was -- not to say that there were not crimes or that they were tolerant, but I do believe that they were less violently intolerant and that there was some space in Sarajevo for those who were not of the majority Muslim community in a way, for example, that there was really no space in Visegrad, when we visited Visegrad, for the non-Serb population. So despite what Mr. Izetbegovic said in the Islamic declaration, during the period in which I lived in Sarajevo, there was some -- some degree of toleration, at least more than there was in the -- in the other areas of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there was an incomparably greater degree of concentration of international institutions, as well as UNPROFOR and non-governmental organisations, and everything else in Sarajevo; isn't that right? In actual fact, Sarajevo was under a magnifying glass held by you, in view of the number of those present, that is to say, the members, the personnel, the staffs of all kinds of international organisations. Isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be the last question. Mr. Harland, is there anything you want to add in relation to that observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just agree with Mr. Milosevic and confirm that in other Bosnian government-controlled territories which were not so much under our scrutiny, the situation was generally rather less tolerant. So I would agree with that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. One at a time. Yes. Time is short, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My only observations were two: First, to say that I should have drawn to your attention that I was assisted in my work with this witness by Ms. Edgerton who sits with me. I'm grateful to her for that. The second, that the protective measure matter, our position is unchanged. We've made our inquiries, There is no change. We can, of course, address you about it orally, but otherwise the matter is as revealed on paper at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll look at that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just briefly, Mr. May. I'm sure you know that for eight days now - today being the eighth day, and you have documentation about that - that I have extremely high blood pressure, and I have been very patient and have been doing my part of the job at each sitting. And you yourself said that for the reasons emphasised by physicians to you that every second weekend be a long weekend. Last weekend was a short weekend, and as it's eight days since my blood pressure has been unacceptably high - but I'm not worrying about that - but I would like to have a longer weekend this coming weekend, extended, in keeping with the ruling you already made with respect to my timetable and schedule. So I'd like Friday and Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there we are, application for more time off. What would the effect be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The effect would be very serious for the witnesses, not least because a witness coming on Monday, who is protected until evidence is given certainly, is I think only available on Monday and into Tuesday and has been the subject of long-standing arrangements. We have, of course, other witnesses, including this witness, who is I know committed to flying home tomorrow afternoon and he's made domestic arrangements in respect of a family member tomorrow night, subject to the hurricane, I suppose, but I'm not sure about that. But he's been here a long time and he's -- he's got those domestic arrangements. And then there are other witnesses who will have to be detained or alternatively sent back and brought back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What -- Mr. Nice, what is the effect? If we do this, what is the effect? If we grant him an adjournment, it means, first of all, we'd probably have to ask this witness to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's the beginning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there's another one who has been here for a week and we were hoping to start tomorrow. That witness is a protected witness. I can't identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But that witness would then -- would then in any event have to be held over in all probabilities while Monday's witness is taken. Alternatively Monday's witness would have to be stood down with no guarantee of when he could come back, and he's an extremely important witness. What Mr. Groome raises as a possible compromise, going through the -- perhaps those witnesses and allowing a break then. I know we already have a break scheduled for the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't accept the -- the accused's mathematics, but nonetheless we obviously have to have some regard to his health.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If -- with regard to this witness - who comes from America and who has made domestic arrangements for tomorrow night. I know there's only two sessions tomorrow, but it would be extremely helpful for him and his family arrangements and so on if he can be back tomorrow and not have to come again. Now, if his evidence could be concluded tomorrow, I can then make inquiries of Monday's witness to see if he's going to be able to accommodate us by, for example, doing Tuesday and Wednesday, and we'll just have to shoulder the expense of all the other witnesses, and in that way it might be possible that a compromise could be arranged by the accused having Monday off, for example, with a view to having Friday off as well so he does a three-day week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We could look at that. We could look at that. And of course, if he is going to make applications of this sort, it's helpful to have it earlier rather than later than springing it on us at the last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll consider that as a possible compromise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've -- we've had to consider very carefully the position. We have to weigh up a number of considerations: The health of the accused, of course, but also the conduct of the trial and the concerns and the considerations of witnesses who come sometimes from a very long way and have to stay here a long time. In those circumstances, the decision we arrive at is this: Mr. Milosevic, you will have -- we must finish this witness's evidence now tomorrow. You will have two sessions in which to do that. So finish that by 12.00. We will then release the witness. We will not sit on Monday, but we will sit again on Tuesday and we will review the position later in the week as to the health of the accused and any other relevant circumstances. We'll adjourn now, until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of September 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
